articles.title: Bangladesh Joins Saudi-led Defense Coalition as Bab el-Mandeb Risks Grow
articles.full_text:
Bangladesh says that joining the Saudi-led defense coalition does not pose a threat to its relations with Iran.
Screenshot of a video posted by the Saudi Arabian Ministry of Defense showing a meeting of officials of 14 countries that joined the maritime defense coalition, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, July 30, 2026.
Bangladesh has joined a Saudi-led maritime defense coalition amid rising tensions in West Asia, which are putting some of the world’s busiest shipping routes via the Red Sea, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and the Gulf of Aden at risk.
The coalition has 14 founding members: Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Pakistan, Turkiye, Egypt, Jordan, Yemen, Bangladesh, Nigeria, Sudan, Djibouti, and Somalia.
Saudi Arabia will lead the coalition and host its headquarters. Its planned activities include intelligence sharing, joint planning, and coordinated maritime operations. However, its charter, command system and rules of engagement have not yet been made public.
The initiative followed attacks on Saudi-linked shipping and a naval blockade announced by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi movement on July 20. The threat became more serious after disruption in the Strait of Hormuz pushed Saudi Arabia to move more oil through Yanbu, its main port on the Red Sea.
This placed greater pressure on the route through Bab el-Mandeb. Saudi Arabia now faces risks around both of the main waterways used to move energy supplies from the Arabian Peninsula.
Bangladesh has backed the coalition, which aims to strengthen maritime security and protect freedom of navigation, international trade routes, and energy supply lines.
Dhaka had condemned the Houthi blockade on July 22, warning that it could threaten regional peace and stability and disrupt global trade and energy supplies. Its decision to join the coalition reflects Bangladesh’s own exposure to trouble in the region.
Bangladesh sends a large share of its exports to Europe. Ships carrying garments and other goods normally use the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. When shipping companies avoid this route, vessels must travel around the Cape of Good Hope. The longer journey increases fuel use, freight charges, insurance costs, and delivery times.
Bangladesh also imports cotton, chemicals, machinery, and industrial materials through the Red Sea and Suez Canal. A prolonged disruption could raise freight costs and put further pressure on production costs and consumer prices.
Saudi Arabia holds a special place in Bangladesh’s foreign relations. The two countries established diplomatic relations in 1975. Bangladeshi labor migration to the kingdom began the following year and has since become one of the main foundations of the relationship. More than 752,000 Bangladeshis went to Saudi Arabia for work in 2025 alone. They accounted for over two-thirds of Bangladesh’s total overseas labor deployment that year.
Naturally, Saudi Arabia is one of Bangladesh’s largest sources of remittances. Bangladeshi workers there sent home about $5.28 billion during the first 11 months of the 2025–26 financial year, equal to roughly 16 percent of total remittance inflows. The money supports household spending on food, education, healthcare, and housing. In addition, the remittances supply U.S. dollars to an economy that frequently faces pressure on its foreign exchange reserves.
Saudi institutions are also involved in Bangladesh’s energy financing. In 2024, the International Islamic Trade Finance Corporation agreed to provide $1.4 billion to the Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation for fuel imports. The Saudi Fund for Development has operated in Bangladesh since 1977.
These interests help explain why Dhaka responded positively to the Saudi proposal. A refusal could have created tension with a country closely linked to Bangladesh’s labor market, remittance earnings, fuel supply, and development finance.
The government has not, however, explained what Bangladesh will contribute to the coalition. There is no public confirmation that Bangladesh will send a warship, aircraft, or combat personnel. It is also unclear whether Dhaka will provide surveillance information, liaison officers, training support, or financial contributions.
However, at a press briefing on 2 August, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s Foreign Affairs Adviser Humayun Kabir said Bangladesh’s decision should not be seen as an anti-Iran move. “We are also talking to Iran, so there is no reason to see this as excluding or hurting Iran in any way,” he said, adding that the coalition was mainly intended to address the Houthi challenge.
Bangladesh may begin with a limited role. It could attend meetings, exchange information, take part in exercises, or assign officers to the coalition headquarters.
There is a precedent for such participation. Bangladesh joined the Saudi-led Islamic Military Counter Terrorism Coalition in 2015 but did not take on a major operational role. The latest coalition could follow a similar course.
However, this time the wider regional setting makes this arrangement more sensitive. The Houthis are aligned with Iran, while Saudi Arabia is one of Iran’s main regional rivals. Riyadh describes the coalition as defensive and says it is not directed against any state. Its actions will determine whether that distinction remains convincing.
Merchant escorts, surveillance, search-and-rescue work, and defensive patrols can be presented as measures to protect navigation. Attacks on Yemeni territory, support for strikes, seizure of Iranian vessels, or participation in a blockade would place Bangladesh much closer to the regional conflict.
Bangladesh has no direct dispute with Iran and continues to maintain cordial relations with Tehran. The economic relationship, however, is limited compared with Bangladesh’s ties with Saudi Arabia. Iran offers no comparable labor market, remittance flows, or development financing.
Dhaka is therefore likely to lean toward Riyadh should its relations with Saudi and Iran conflict.
Much will depend on how Bangladesh defines the limits of its participation once the coalition becomes operational. The financial costs and rules governing intelligence sharing have also not been disclosed.
Greater security along major shipping routes could reduce the risk of sharp increases in freight, insurance, and energy costs. More predictable shipping could also help exporters avoid delays, particularly in the garment sector.
However, membership itself is unlikely to have a direct effect on domestic fuel prices or transport fares. These are also shaped by global commodity prices, exchange rates, taxation, and domestic energy policy. There is similarly no indication that participation in the coalition will lead to more employment opportunities for Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia.
Security cooperation could bring Dhaka and Riyadh even closer. Their relationship already rests heavily on labor migration, remittances, energy financing, and development assistance.
For Bangladesh, much will depend on what role it actually takes in the coalition. Helping protect commercial shipping is one thing; taking part in military operations linked to the wider conflict would be quite another.
Until the coalition’s mandate, command structure and Bangladesh’s specific responsibilities become clearer, it remains difficult to determine how significant the decision will be for Dhaka.
Bangladesh has joined a Saudi-led maritime defense coalition amid rising tensions in West Asia, which are putting some of the world’s busiest shipping routes via the Red Sea, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and the Gulf of Aden at risk.
articles.summary: Bangladesh says that joining the Saudi-led defense coalition does not pose a threat to its relations with Iran.

articles.title: Why Pakistan Is Pleased With Its Counterterrorism Dialogue With the US
articles.full_text:
If the early rounds of talks focused on terror threats to U.S. security, the last two rounds included discussion of the BLA and TTP  – threats to Pakistan’s security.
Delegations of the U.S. and Pakistan at the Fourth Counterterrorism Dialogue in Washington, D.C., Aug. 5, 2026.
Pakistan and the United States held the fourth round of their annual Counterterrorism Dialogue in Washington, D.C., on August 4. The Pakistani delegation was led by Ambassador Nabeel Munir, special secretary at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, while Ambassador Gregory LoGerfo, the U.S. coordinator for counterterrorism, led the American side.
The joint statement issued at the end of the talks underscored their shared strategic interests in the counterterrorism partnership and determination to confront regional security threats. “The United States and Pakistan affirmed their joint resolve to confront terrorist organizations that endanger the safety of their citizens and the stability of the region, including ISIS-Khorasan (ISIS-K), al-Qa’ida (AQ), the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), and the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) and its affiliates,” it said, emphasizing that their counterterrorism collaboration was “to keep both of their nations safe and secure, and as part of an enduring vision of regional peace, prosperity, and stability.”
The institutionalization of this annual bilateral mechanism demonstrates that counterterrorism continues to serve as a crucial pillar of Pakistan-U.S. relations, which has long survived broader geopolitical shifts. Since the dialogue’s inauguration in 2023, the platform has steadily evolved into a structured security partnership.
Pre-2023, bilateral security and counterterrorism exchanges were routinely subsumed under broader umbrella frameworks, such as the U.S.-Pakistan Strategic Dialogue or various Defense Consultative Group sessions. On these forums, counterterrorism imperatives often competed with larger and at times competing agendas.
At the inaugural session of this dialogue in 2023, its primary function was to re-establish structured and formal engagement amid the post-2021 regional posture shift triggered by the withdrawal of U.S. forces from Afghanistan.
The U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan temporarily sapped momentum from the Pakistan-U.S. bilateral security cooperation. The 2023 dialogue, therefore, served primarily to establish a baseline for bilateral security contact by maintaining a broad focus on general regional stability. Moreover, the 2023 session also focused on areas where the two countries can collaborate to counter all forms of violent extremism and combat terrorism financing.
During the second session in 2024, both delegations refined the framework’s focus by prioritizing TTP and ISIS-K, also known as Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP), as key regional threats. The joint statement highlighted these outfits as key challenges to regional stability, noting that “The United States and Pakistan recognize that a partnership to counter ISIS-Khorasan, TTP, and other terrorist organizations will advance security in the region.”
In 2025, the dialogue reached an important turning point when the joint statement formally integrated the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) alongside the TTP and ISKP. For Islamabad, securing explicit recognition of the BLA as a threat within a formal U.S. security dialogue marked a major diplomatic victory. Following a wave of high-profile BLA-led militant attacks in Pakistan, Islamabad had consistently pushed for Washington to recognize the group’s violence as a primary threat that required bilateral counterterrorism focus.
The fourth round in 2026 has further expanded the operational scope of cooperation by reintroducing al-Qaida into the explicit joint threat environment, alongside ISKP, the TTP, the BLA, and its affiliates. From the U.S. perspective, the inclusion of al-Qaida highlights persistent concerns in Washington regarding core militant networks that continue to operate in the region, particularly from Afghanistan.
Tracking the dialogue’s four-year trajectory illustrates a notable shift in bilateral security dynamics between Islamabad and Washington.
Arguably, the sessions in 2023 and 2024 were largely shaped by Washington’s primary counterterrorism priorities following its withdrawal from Afghanistan. During this phase, U.S. interests focused on broader regional security threats, including monitoring transnational terrorist elements and tackling issues related to countering terrorism financing.
However, the 2025 and 2026 dialogues reflect a far more balanced trade-off between the two countries. These were not just about the threats that concerned the United States. The 2025 and 2026 talks saw the U.S. formally acknowledge Pakistan’s core internal security challenges, most notably the threats posed by the BLA and TTP.
The explicit inclusion of Pakistan-centric security threats like the TTP and BLA reflects a meaningful improvement in bilateral relations.
Going forward, Pakistan’s strategic objective will likely involve translating these joint statements into concrete and operational support. Islamabad has consistently sought expanded U.S. cooperation to dismantle cross-border sanctuaries in Afghanistan and secure official UN sanctions against top BLA and TTP leadership.
In this regard, getting the U.S. to put tangible pressure on regional facilitators of BLA and TTP attacks by disrupting these groups’ international funding streams and operational networks would mark the next key breakthrough for this evolving bilateral partnership under the ongoing counter terrorism dialogue.

articles.title: Myanmar Nationals Face Deportation From US After Court Ruling
articles.full_text:
The ruling follows a Supreme Court decision in June that limited courts’ ability to challenge TPS designations.
A U.S. federal judge has cleared the way for President Donald Trump’s administration to end temporary protected status (TPS) for nearly 4,000 people from Myanmar, presaging their possible arrest and deportation.
In a ruling on Friday, U.S. District Judge Matthew Kennelly of the Northern District of Illinois rejected last-minute efforts by immigrant rights advocates to maintain the TPS designations. The ruling came just hours after a federal judge in Boston handed down a similar ruling rejecting a challenge from an immigrant-advocacy organization against the removal of TPS status from around 232 South Sudanese nationals.
Both rulings referenced a U.S. Supreme Court decision from June, which ruled that the administration had the authority to end similar protections for thousands of people from Haiti and Syria. The Supreme Court ruling limited lower courts’ ability to block DHS’ efforts to end TPS for people from roughly a dozen countries, arguing that federal judges had no authority to weigh in on a challenge to TPS terminations.
TPS was created by the U.S. Congress in 1990, and protects non-U.S. citizens from deportation to countries facing armed conflict or other crises posing a threat to their safety. It also grants them authorization to work in the U.S.
The TPS designation for Myanmar was granted for the first time after the 2021 military coup, which was followed by a nationwide uprising against military rule. The ongoing civil war and military repression have wrecked Myanmar’s economy, displaced more than 3.5 million people, and pushed tens of thousands more to flee the country. There are around 4,000 Myanmar nationals currently in the U.S. under the TPS program.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) revoked TPS status for Myanmar in November of last year, citing the military junta’s upcoming elections as evidence that the country had “made notable progress in governance and stability.” The TPS designation for Myanmar was originally set to expire in January, but court orders kept the protections in place while a class-action lawsuit challenged the DHS decision.
While the Trump administration said that the revocation of TPS status was justified by improvements in Myanmar’s political situation, plaintiffs argued in their lawsuit that the decision failed to account for the real conditions in Myanmar, where conflict and military repression continue unabated, and was just one aspect of a broader campaign to end TPS designations.
During Trump’s second term, the DHS has revoked TPS protections for hundreds of thousands of migrants from countries including Afghanistan, Cameroon, Haiti, Honduras, Nepal, Nicaragua, Syria, South Sudan, and Venezuela.
In addition to losing their ability to work in the U.S., the 4,000 Myanmar nationals now face possible arrest and deportation. According to one report, many of these Myanmar nationals have lived and worked in the United States since fleeing the country; some have even raised U.S. citizen children.
In a statement issued after the ruling, the International Refugee Assistance Project described the decision as “devastating” for these individuals.
“The court’s decision to allow TPS protections to lapse puts thousands of Burmese TPS holders in grave danger,” said Dinesh McCoy, a staff attorney at the Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund who was lead counsel in the case. “It is unconscionable for the Trump administration to gamble with their lives as part of its larger campaign to use immigration policy as a tool for racial exclusion.”
Thura Doe, a plaintiff in the lawsuit, said that he was “devastated” by the court’s ruling and “terrified of what will happen if I’m forced to return to Burma.”
McCoy said that his organization was “continuing to explore all available legal options.”

TPS was created by the U.S. Congress in 1990, and protects non-U.S. citizens from deportation to countries facing armed conflict or other crises posing a threat to their safety. It also grants them authorization to work in the U.S.
The TPS designation for Myanmar was granted for the first time after the 2021 military coup, which was followed by a nationwide uprising against military rule. The ongoing civil war and military repression have wrecked Myanmar’s economy, displaced more than 3.5 million people, and pushed tens of thousands more to flee the country. There are around 4,000 Myanmar nationals currently in the U.S. under the TPS program.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) revoked TPS status for Myanmar in November of last year, citing the military junta’s upcoming elections as evidence that the country had “made notable progress in governance and stability.” The TPS designation for Myanmar was originally set to expire in January, but court orders kept the protections in place while a class-action lawsuit challenged the DHS decision.
While the Trump administration said that the revocation of TPS status was justified by improvements in Myanmar’s political situation, plaintiffs argued in their lawsuit that the decision failed to account for the real conditions in Myanmar, where conflict and military repression continue unabated, and was just one aspect of a broader campaign to end TPS designations.
During Trump’s second term, the DHS has revoked TPS protections for hundreds of thousands of migrants from countries including Afghanistan, Cameroon, Haiti, Honduras, Nepal, Nicaragua, Syria, South Sudan, and Venezuela.
In addition to losing their ability to work in the U.S., the 4,000 Myanmar nationals now face possible arrest and deportation. According to one report, many of these Myanmar nationals have lived and worked in the United States since fleeing the country; some have even raised U.S. citizen children.
In a statement issued after the ruling, the International Refugee Assistance Project described the decision as “devastating” for these individuals.
“The court’s decision to allow TPS protections to lapse puts thousands of Burmese TPS holders in grave danger,” said Dinesh McCoy, a staff attorney at the Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund who was lead counsel in the case. “It is unconscionable for the Trump administration to gamble with their lives as part of its larger campaign to use immigration policy as a tool for racial exclusion.”
Thura Doe, a plaintiff in the lawsuit, said that he was “devastated” by the court’s ruling and “terrified of what will happen if I’m forced to return to Burma.”
McCoy said that his organization was “continuing to explore all available legal options.”
A U.S. federal judge has cleared the way for President Donald Trump’s administration to end temporary protected status (TPS) for nearly 4,000 people from Myanmar, presaging their possible arrest and deportation.
In a ruling on Friday, U.S. District Judge Matthew Kennelly of the Northern District of Illinois rejected last-minute efforts by immigrant rights advocates to maintain the TPS designations. The ruling came just hours after a federal judge in Boston handed down a similar ruling rejecting a challenge from an immigrant-advocacy organization against the removal of TPS status from around 232 South Sudanese nationals.
Sebastian Strangio is Southeast Asia editor at The Diplomat.
articles.summary: The ruling follows a Supreme Court decision in June that limited courts' ability to challenge TPS designations.

articles.title: The Quiet Vietnamese
articles.full_text:
Landlocked Laos needs counterweights to its massive neighbor, China, if is to avoid being paralyzed by debt. The most obvious choice is Vietnam.
The border gate between Vietnam and Laos at Lao Bao, Vietnam.
Vietnamese investment in Laos didn’t just grow in the first half of 2026. It nearly quadrupled.
Vietnam’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs put first-quarter investment at $582 million, up 4.2 times year-on-year, with cumulative Vietnamese investment reaching $6.6 billion across 289 projects. Lao officials, speaking at July’s VIETLAO Expo in Vientiane, gave a slightly higher H1 figure of nearly $600 million, but still a 4.2-fold jump, mostly in mining, electricity, energy, and agriculture. An earlier count from March, reported by the Asia News Network, put cumulative Vietnamese state-enterprise investment at $6.21 billion across 276 projects. It confirmed Laos as Vietnam’s top outbound destination among 85 countries.
VietnamNet reported Vietnam-Laos trade turnover of $1.07 billion in the first five months of 2026 (Vietnam exporting $293 million, importing $782 million), with both governments, according to the Voice of Vietnam’s coverage of the Expo, targeting $4 billion in bilateral trade for 2026 on the way to a stated goal of $10 billion by 2030.
Official discussion of this topic is typically framed in terms of “great friendship,” “special solidarity,” and “strategic cohesion.” Some version of these mantras has been circulating between Vietnamese and Lao officials since the mid-1970s, and nothing in recent statements from Hanoi or Vientiane signifies an imminent break in convention.
But the timing of this particular surge in investment is interesting, and reading it purely as fraternal solidarity between neighbors is naïve. The reality is that Laos is in a debt crisis, and it knows it. The small land-locked country’s trying carefully, and on its own terms, to reduce how much of its economic future drifts into the hands of Beijing.
Start with the numbers that don’t get quoted in the friendship-society press releases. The Bertelsmann Transformation Index’s 2026 Laos country report puts public debt at $16.4 billion, or 108 percent of GDP by IMF estimates, and warns that annual debt service is set to climb past $700 million a year by 2028 – a figure it says will likely require debt relief from China “on an unprecedented scale.” 9DASHLINE puts Laos’s specific debt exposure to Beijing, its largest single bilateral lender, at around $12.2 billion, or roughly 65 percent of GDP.
Coface’s country risk analysis notes that foreign direct investment, which totaled around 5 percent of GDP in 2024, still comes mainly from China, Thailand, and Vietnam, and mostly flows into the hydropower dams, the mining sector, and grid infrastructure. Against that backdrop, Vientiane went back to the international bond market in November 2025 for the first time in years, raising $300 million in Singapore at an 11.25 percent coupon – a rate that, as the East Asia Forum noted in its February country review, reflects investor concern over prior negative-pledge violations on hydropower assets and continued opacity around Chinese debt deferrals.
China has granted partial debt deferrals, which the same East Asia Forum review says buys Vientiane breathing room without resolving anything, although it expects a more comprehensive debt restructuring sometime in 2026. A separate East Asia Forum piece from March describes how the new leadership installed after January’s 12th Party Congress has formalized “self-reliance” and partner diversification as explicit policy. Laos is not dropping China, which remains structurally impossible given the scale of existing projects like the Laos-China Railway and China Southern Power Grid’s stake in the national grid, but it is no longer content to be a single-supplier economy either.
The Lowy Institute, in its own assessment of Laos’s debt crisis, cautions that the “debt trap” framing is overstated, and that Lao elites bear real responsibility for the borrowing decisions and the collapse in revenue collection that followed. But it agrees China has built dominant infrastructural and geoeconomic power over Laos over roughly two decades, even as Vientiane keeps trying to balance that against Vietnam, Thailand, Russia, and others.
Vietnam is one of two partners Laos is visibly leaning on to execute that diversification. The other, less discussed in the ASEAN business press but just as real, is Russia. The East Asia Forum piece from March notes seven wide-ranging agreements signed in Moscow, including a defense cooperation roadmap, since the start of the year. Neither relationship is a substitute for China’s role in Lao infrastructure. What both offer instead is a hedge: additional capital sources, additional political cover, and – in Vietnam’s case particularly – additional legitimacy, since the Hanoi-Vientiane relationship carries decades of party-to-party trust that no amount of Chinese financing can replicate.
That’s the real function of the investment surge. Vietnam isn’t displacing China in Laos; the two economies aren’t even competing for the same assets. Vietnamese capital is concentrated in mining, hydropower and energy, and high-value agriculture: sectors where Vietnamese firms already have regional experience and where the investment tends to be smaller-ticket and faster to deploy than the multi-billion-dollar rail and grid projects China has built. China’s footprint, by contrast, sits in the capital-intensive, decade-horizon infrastructure that defines the physical shape of the Lao economy, such as the national power grid and the railway linking Vientiane to Kunming. Those aren’t going anywhere, and nothing in the current Vietnam-Laos push is designed to touch them.
What Vietnam is doing is filling the gaps around this Chinese infrastructure. These are gaps that are being filled with Vientiane’s encouragement. A 2026 academic assessment of the relationship by Khanh Tran, Hoan Quang Truong, and Hoa Le Phuong argues that the Vietnam-Laos “strategic connection” now explicitly contains elements of competition with China and the exertion of Vietnamese influence, alongside — not instead of — the fraternal solidarity language, as both countries navigate the pressure that a more assertive China is putting on the wider Mekong subregion.
VIETLAO Expo is worth keeping an eye on because trade fairs are usually where the real texture of a relationship can be seen before it shows up in the communiqués. VietnamPlus reported that Vientiane’s July edition drew more than 250 booths and 140 companies from both sides – a bigger showing than in previous years.
VietnamNet’s coverage of the accompanying business seminar quoted a Vietnam Trade Promotion Agency official calling for stronger direct business links and better cross-border logistics: better roads, better customs processing, and fewer middlemen skimming margins off cross-border trade.
The same VietnamNet report had Lao officials explicitly encouraging more Vietnamese investment in organic agriculture and deep processing, which can broadly refer to refining goods into finished or semi-finished states prior to export, a higher-value activity than the raw resource extraction that has defined so much of Laos’s relationship with China.

If Laos can successfully renegotiate its China debt while continuing to scale up Vietnamese investment, it may be able to start to genuinely diversify its way out of dependency, avoiding the concession of state assets to Chinese buyers to plug near-term liquidity gaps. That is a lingering problem with mining concessions and state-owned enterprises. In other words, ideally, Vietnamese investment becomes a real hedge against predatory Chinese business practices.

articles.title: Myanmar Rejects ASEAN Call for Suu Kyi’s Release, Questions Need For Special Envoy
articles.full_text:
The military-backed government is pushing for full readmission to ASEAN, while rejecting outright the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus initiative.
Myanmar’s military-backed government has again rejected the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)’s call for the release of detained leader Aung San Suu Kyi and dismissed the need for an ASEAN special envoy on Myanmar.
The statement came on Saturday, after the 11-nation Southeast Asian bloc renewed its call for the “unconditional release” of the 81-year-old leader, who was removed from power in the February 2021 coup and remains under house arrest in Naypyidaw.
On August 3, Aung San Suu Kyi was permitted to meet with a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and the military authorities released four photos of the meeting.
In an ASEAN Chair’s Statement dated August 7, ASEAN welcomed the meeting, describing it as “a positive step towards inclusive national dialogue and reconciliation,” but urged greater access to political detainees and reiterated its call for Suu Kyi’s “complete and unconditional release.” It also renewed its earlier request that current special envoy on Myanmar, Philippine Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro, be allowed to meet with Aung San Suu Kyi on her next mission to the country.
In a statement on Saturday, Myanmar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs rejected the ASEAN Chair’s request, echoing the denial that it made to an earlier request from Lazaro in late June.
“Although the government has commuted her sentences based on humanitarian considerations, the matter of a full and unconditional release shall only be carried out in accordance with the law,” it said.
After being removed in the coup in February 2021, Aung San Suu Kyi was charged with a range of far-fetched charges, including incitement, corruption, election fraud, and violation of Myanmar’s Official Secrets Act. Despite being granted several sentence reductions, she still has more than 18 years to serve in prison.
The Ministry added that the government will continue working with Lazaro for the remainder of her term, but doesn’t see the need to continue down that path when Singapore takes over ASEAN’s rotating chairmanship at the start of 2027.
“At present, the government, which emerged from the multiparty democratic elections reflecting the genuine will of the people, has assumed state responsibility,” the statement said. “Therefore, Myanmar is of the view that the appointment and the continued role of the new Special Envoy of the ASEAN Chair are no longer necessary.”
The statement concluded by saying that Myanmar would “take appropriate countermeasures, on a case-by-case basis” in response to “unconstructive and discriminatory treatment” by ASEAN or any of its member states.
ASEAN has barred Myanmar from its summits since late 2021, over its failure to implement its Five-Point Consensus plan for resolving the country’s conflict. This involved pledges to cease violence, allow humanitarian access, and engage in political dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
Since assuming the office of president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has led a push for a normalization of Myanmar’s relationship ASEAN. In late April, in an apparent effort to placate skeptical member states, his administration announced Aung San Suu Kyi’s relocation from prison to house arrest and announced an amnesty of political prisoners. In this effort, it has enjoyed the strong support of neighbor Thailand, which hosted Min Aung Hlaing with full state honors last week. During the visit, the Thai government “reaffirmed its commitment to supporting and continuing to work closely with Myanmar for Myanmar’s full and equal participation in ASEAN mechanisms and processes.”
But rather than making even some cursory efforts at implementing the Five-Point Consensus, as one might expect, Naypyidaw has grown more defiant. In a speech on July 31, Min Aung Hlaing declared that the Consensus was “not the consensus of all ASEAN member states” and was therefore invalid. This came after the military-dominated Union Parliament last month passed a resolution rejecting the plan as an unwarranted interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs, stating that it “does not align with the current political developments in Myanmar.”
Officially, ASEAN continues to adhere to the Five-Point Consensus, which it says offers the only route toward normalization for Myanmar. Lazaro said last month that due to Myanmar’s lack of efforts at implementing the agreement, its full reintegration with ASEAN was still “far off.”
There is no obvious way out of the current deadlock. Myanmar is probably hoping that it can outwait ASEAN, perhaps banking on a more supportive chair when Thailand takes the bloc’s helm in 2028. Given the wavering opinion within ASEAN about the best means of dealing with the Myanmar issue, and the growing push for some kind of re-engagement, its expectations are not necessarily misplaced.

articles.title: The Murder of a Uyghur in America Spotlights the Dangers for the Diaspora
articles.full_text:
China’s transnational repression is real, and host governments themselves are now playing a role in pressuring Uyghur communities.
A women holding the flag of East Turkestan in Ankara, Turkiye, Oct. 1, 2023.
At 10:15 p.m. on July 29, Shukur Aikebaer was abducted and murdered outside his residence in Chino County, California, by two individuals, reportedly named Zhengfeng Bo and Jianquan Bo. Aikebaer’s death sent shock waves through Uyghur communities worldwide. 
Investigators have not established a motive or released details about the suspects; Zhengfeng Bo was killed by police during the kidnapping. However, the incident mirrors a similar case from Uzbekistan. In July 2024, Ablehet Qahar, an Uyghur historian, was murdered in his Tashkent apartment. The crime was quietly swept under the rug, and shortly after, Qahar’s residence was barricaded and the entirety of his Uyghur historical collections disappeared. 
Together, the two deaths underscore a reality many Uyghurs know well: that physical distance from Xinjiang – called East Turkestan by many of the region’s native Uyghur people – no longer guarantees their safety.
Over the past decade, the People’s Republic of China has dramatically expanded its efforts to stifle the voices of Uyghurs outside its borders. Reports of surveillance, harassment, threats to family, and attempted deportations have become familiar features of diaspora life. Collectively, such practices are understood as transnational repression – the effort by governments to monitor and coerce individuals living outside their territorial jurisdiction.
But focusing only on Beijing’s direct actions misses a larger shift that is unfolding globally, notably in Central Asia.
Most discussions of transnational repression emphasize the sending state’s own actions, whether these be intelligence services, diplomatic pressure, cyber surveillance, or direct intimidation. However, China’s growing political and economic influence appears to be producing a different dynamic, one in which repression is carried out also through the institutions of partner governments. It is, in effect, a form of transnational repression by proxy.
Home to one of the world’s largest Uyghur diasporas, Central Asia has long been central to preserving Uyghur language and culture. However, in recent years the atmosphere has changed. The last few decades in foreign policy have repositioned Central Asia’s importance on the international stage, with the region now reemerging as a key bridge between East Asia and the West. China’s rising economic footprint has sculpted Beijing into an increasingly influential actor in shaping both the foreign policy and the domestic priorities of Central Asian states.
Today, half of the economic corridors within China’s Belt and Road Initiative rely on Central Asian soil and support, making the former Soviet republics of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan vital arteries in China’s push for worldwide connectivity. The tight-knit relationship has brought significant economic benefits but has also created incentives for governments to accommodate Beijing’s concerns – including those involving Uyghur communities.
In Tashkent, my field interviews in 2024 revealed a sharp decline in Uyghur cultural identity over the past five years. Across all interviews conducted in Uzbekistan, community members noted a drastic decline in Uyghur language use and preservation in the past year, particularly among Uyghur youth. Many described a shift away from using Uyghur in public and semi-public environments, especially in contexts where visibility to authorities was a concern. 
Several interviewees reported perceived changes in important cultural hubs. The Tashkent Uyghur National Cultural Center, for example, has now begun sharing its space with representatives of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), a Chinese state-backed organization that has been utilized to “project power and influence beyond China’s borders.” After the introduction of an SCO presence, Uyghur language classes ceased, and youth groups were no longer able to use the space as they once had. Visitors also described increased monitoring inside the building. 
The same sentiment emerged when discussing political symbolism. One community member explained: “We don’t have our motherland’s flag up. We cannot. If we hang it from the window or outside, we will get trouble from the Uzbek authorities, maybe face arrest. It is not well-received.”
The interviewee also cited an escalation in the targeting of Uyghur historical material and ancient records: “Let me tell you of the case of [Uyghur elder in community]. If you go to his house, it is full to the brim with ancient Uyghur texts, books, and writings. That man, though, he is old now… So those books will be thrown away. Actually, they are coerced into throwing away things like this.”
The existence of these collections points to an earlier period in which cultural retention within private spaces remained viable. However, such continuity appears progressively under strain in recent years. The reported coercion to discard such items demonstrates a change from passive erosion to more active forms of interruption enforced by authority.
The situation in Kazakhstan is more complicated.
In 2025, the country was named as one of China’s clients in the Geedge Networks “Great Firewall” leak, which exposed China’s exportation of highly advanced censorship and surveillance infrastructure. The systems and specific technology being sold abroad are extensions of the same digital governance architecture first utilized and refined in the Uyghur homeland, one of the most surveilled regions in the world.
Reflecting this development in China-Kazakhstan relations, fieldwork on Uyghurs in Kazakhstan has resulted in both scrutiny and opposition from local authorities. Several interviewees later reported being threatened and barred from maintaining contact with the researcher. Such experiences reflect the broader climate of securitization and severe surveillance surrounding Uyghur communities and identity preservation – even outside of China’s borders.
Similar to Uzbekistan, Uyghur community members in Kazakhstan also described state-enforced methods of linguistic destruction and cultural eradication. “We teach in Cyrillic,” one interviewee said. “It’s not allowed to teach the Uyghur [Arabic] script to the kids or have any educational material published and printed out in Uyghur [Arabic] script.”
By restricting education to Cyrillic, the Kazakh government effectively forces Uyghur linguistic practice into a state-regulated framework, part of a larger process of depoliticization and controlled assimilation. The prohibition also weakens Uyghurs’ access to the Arabic script that links them to both their literary heritage and contemporary developments in their homeland. While the Uyghur language is under increasing pressure in China, when it is used, it is written with the Arabic script.
Extending further than curricula issues, the concept of Uyghur education in itself has proven to be a problem in recent years. “I gave up on my dream of being a police officer,” one interviewee confided. “It says I am Uyghur on my ID. And I went to Uyghur school. It’s almost like an unsaid rule. They will not hire Uyghurs like this for government positions; it’s not allowed.”
The person’s mention of an “unsaid rule” points to a form of informal but widely understood discrimination. If attendance at a Uyghur school is treated as a disqualifying characteristic, it suggests that language has become politicized in a way that renders it incompatible with state integration. Uyghur has been recast as a marker of exclusion from the political community.
Ultimately, transnational repression represents a new frontier in authoritarian governance, and this evolution has implications that reach far beyond the Uyghur community. For years, Western governments have treated China’s human rights abuses and China’s geopolitical rise as parallel challenges requiring separate policy responses. Central Asia suggests both pose the same challenge. In addition to its effects on regional politics and economics, Beijing’s growing influence is expanding the reach of its human rights agenda beyond China’s borders. If policymakers fail to recognize that connection, they risk confronting China’s repression where it begins rather than where it is already taking hold.

Most discussions of transnational repression emphasize the sending state’s own actions, whether these be intelligence services, diplomatic pressure, cyber surveillance, or direct intimidation. However, China’s growing political and economic influence appears to be producing a different dynamic, one in which repression is carried out also through the institutions of partner governments. It is, in effect, a form of transnational repression by proxy.
Home to one of the world’s largest Uyghur diasporas, Central Asia has long been central to preserving Uyghur language and culture. However, in recent years the atmosphere has changed. The last few decades in foreign policy have repositioned Central Asia’s importance on the international stage, with the region now reemerging as a key bridge between East Asia and the West. China’s rising economic footprint has sculpted Beijing into an increasingly influential actor in shaping both the foreign policy and the domestic priorities of Central Asian states.
articles.summary: China’s transnational repression is real, and host governments themselves are now playing a role in pressuring Uyghur communities.

articles.title: The Iran-US War a Win for China? Not So Fast.
articles.full_text:
The war is also creating strategic opportunities for Washington and new challenges for Beijing in the Middle East.
Two U.S. Navy guided-missile destroyers conducted operations as U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) forces began setting conditions for clearing mines in the Strait of Hormuz, April 11, 2026.
Following the outbreak of the Iran-U.S. conflict on February 28, a prevailing view emerged in international discourse that China was the primary beneficiary of the crisis. This perception was reinforced after Washington and Tehran formally signed a ceasefire agreement and launched follow-on negotiations, prompting many observers to conclude that the United States had suffered a major strategic setback while China had secured significant diplomatic, economic, and geopolitical gains. 
However, a broader assessment of the evolving realities facing the United States, China, Iran, and the wider Middle East suggests that the situation cannot be simply characterized as a case of American failure and Chinese success. On the contrary, as the regional order enters a new phase of adjustment, China may confront a growing number of challenges, while the United States may discover new strategic opportunities.
The conflict undoubtedly imposed costs on the United States’ international image and diplomatic credibility. Despite committing substantial resources to the confrontation, Washington failed to achieve its primary strategic objectives. As the war continued, key U.S. partners in the Middle East, including Israel and several Gulf Arab states, remained exposed to Iranian military pressure and security threats, increasing the overall strategic burden on the United States.
Following the cessation of hostilities, Washington faced mounting pressure from different partners. On one hand, policy differences between the United States and Israel widened considerably, with Israel urging the U.S. to maintain or even intensify pressure on Iran. On the other hand, some Gulf Arab states became increasingly dissatisfied with the U.S. inability to provide effective security guarantees and began reassessing the U.S.-centered regional security architecture that had emerged after the Cold War. Collectively, these developments weakened Washington’s regional standing and international credibility to some extent.
China, by contrast, achieved notable diplomatic gains during the crisis. Economically, Beijing was largely insulated from the worst effects of oil-price volatility and imported inflation. Thanks to a diversified energy import strategy and relatively ample strategic reserves, China successfully mitigated the impact of turbulence in global energy markets and maintained overall domestic economic stability.
Diplomatically, China actively promoted dialogue and de-escalation after the outbreak of the conflict. Beijing maintained close communication with Gulf Arab states, Iran, and Pakistan, while also remaining engaged with the United States on relevant issues, demonstrating considerable diplomatic flexibility and coordination capacity. At the same time, countries such as Pakistan played a constructive role in facilitating contacts between Washington and Tehran and narrowing differences between the two sides. Through the efforts of multiple parties, the United States and Iran eventually reached a ceasefire agreement and launched a new negotiating process. Although China was not a direct participant in the negotiations, it contributed positively to creating a favorable diplomatic environment and reducing tensions. As a result, China’s regional influence and diplomatic reputation in the Middle East were further enhanced.
Nevertheless, characterizing the conflict simply as a Chinese victory and an American defeat risks overlooking the complex realities of the Middle East and the different opportunities and constraints facing both powers. While the United States incurred political and reputational costs in the short term, it continues to occupy a central position within the regional security architecture and retains substantial room for maneuver in security cooperation, technology partnerships, energy exports, and future participation in Iran’s economic reconstruction. 
China, meanwhile, has gained diplomatic prestige and influence but may face increasingly difficult policy choices as disputes surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, regional security arrangements, and the regional economic environment continue to evolve.
The United States: Strategic Damage Control and New Opportunities
For Washington, the end of the war did not produce the regime change in Iran that some policymakers initially envisioned, nor did it compel Tehran to make comprehensive concessions. However, after several months of conflict, the United States opted to limit further costs and adjust its approach on issues including Iran’s nuclear program, regional security, sanctions policy, and the governance of the Strait of Hormuz.
These adjustments ultimately enabled Washington and Tehran to reach a memorandum of understanding, terminate active hostilities, and initiate a new diplomatic process. Although there have been recurring clashes since then, as both sides accuse each other of failing to honor the deal, talks are continuing through intermediaries. While the U.S. failed to achieve all of its objectives, it has also avoided giving up major concessions to Iran.
From a regional security perspective, the war has not fundamentally weakened Washington’ influence in the Middle East. In some respects, it reinforced security cooperation between Washington and its regional partners. Although some Gulf Arab states have begun questioning the U.S. ability to provide long-term security guarantees and have expressed concern that close military cooperation with Washington may expose them to regional conflicts, countries such as the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain still lack a viable alternative security partner capable of replacing the United States.
Facing continued threats from Iranian missiles and unmanned systems, these states have expanded cooperation with Washington in areas such as air-defense systems, intelligence sharing, and military technology. As a result, the United States has largely preserved – and in some respects strengthened – its dominant security position in the Gulf.
This security relationship is also expanding into technology and infrastructure cooperation. Modern air defense networks, military applications of artificial intelligence, and digital security architectures require supporting infrastructure including data centers, computing capacity, and advanced communications systems. Consequently, Gulf Arab states are likely to deepen cooperation with the United States in artificial intelligence, big data applications, digital infrastructure, and network development while increasingly adopting American technological standards and regulatory frameworks.
This trend provides Washington with opportunities not only to maintain traditional security partnerships but also to generate new strategic and economic benefits through technology cooperation, digital infrastructure projects, and industrial collaboration, thereby reinforcing its long-term regional influence.
Furthermore, neither the Strait of Hormuz issue nor the Iranian nuclear question necessarily poses a direct challenge to Washington’s core strategic interests. The United States does not depend directly on Hormuz transit routes for domestic energy security. Since 2018, the U.S. has become one of the world’s leading energy producers and has significantly reduced its reliance on Middle Eastern energy supplies.
During the conflict, particularly when shipping through the Strait of Hormuz faced disruptions, several energy-importing countries sought more reliable suppliers. Japan, South Korea, and others consequently increased energy imports from the United States. The resulting volatility in energy markets enhanced the strategic value of American energy exports and strengthened U.S. influence within global energy markets.
In short, although the United States failed to fully resolve the Iran challenge through military means, it nonetheless secured a range of strategic benefits by maintaining its dominant security role, expanding technology and infrastructure partnerships, and strengthening its position in global energy markets.
China: Diplomatic Constraints and Economic Challenges
For China, the Iran-U.S. conflict and its subsequent political arrangements have created a new set of diplomatic and strategic challenges. The war not only deepened divisions among Gulf Arab states but also complicated China’s long-term multilateral diplomacy in the Middle East. As regional tensions intensified, the China-Arab States Summit originally planned for June was postponed indefinitely, reflecting the growing complexity of the regional political environment.
Among the emerging challenges, the Strait of Hormuz issue is likely to be one of the most sensitive. Following the conflict, Iranian domestic opinion shifted significantly, reinforcing political support for Tehran’s claims regarding the Strait of Hormuz and adjacent waters in the Persian Gulf. Since the 1950s, many of Iran’s claims concerning maritime rights and territorial issues in the Gulf have been codified through domestic legal instruments. Moreover, because Iran has not formally ratified the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, international arguments regarding unrestricted freedom of navigation do not necessarily enjoy broad legal or political acceptance within Iran.
Under these circumstances, Tehran’s efforts to strengthen its control over the Strait of Hormuz and potentially institutionalize transit fees or passage charges could become a long-term policy trend. Such demands possess substantial domestic political support and are closely tied to Iran’s strategic and security calculations.
For China, this creates a difficult policy dilemma. As the world’s largest energy importer, a major shipbuilding nation, and a leading maritime trading power, China depends heavily on the stability and security of critical sea lanes such as the Strait of Hormuz. How Beijing responds to Iran’s evolving claims regarding Hormuz will become a major test of its Middle East policy.
Supporting Iranian demands could damage China’s relations with Gulf Arab states, particularly the UAE. Conversely, openly opposing Tehran’s position could negatively affect Sino-Iranian relations. Consequently, balancing energy security, freedom of navigation, and relations with both Iran and Gulf Arab states is likely to become an increasingly difficult diplomatic challenge for Beijing.
China may also face adjustments in the region’s economic and technological landscape. Growing cooperation between the United States and Gulf Arab states in military technology, military applications of artificial intelligence, and data infrastructure could gradually reduce opportunities for Chinese firms in advanced technology sectors. Given Washington’s tendency to promote exclusive cooperation arrangements in areas such as AI, big data, and digital infrastructure, the scope of China-Gulf technological cooperation may become increasingly constrained.
At the same time, if Iran and the United States reach a settlement that involves easing sanctions on Iran, substantial Western investment and commercial projects could enter the Iranian market. China’s long-standing economic advantages in Iran may therefore weaken. In sectors such as energy development, infrastructure construction, and financial services, Chinese companies could face significantly greater competition from American and European firms.
From a military perspective, although Gulf Arab states have sought to diversify aspects of their external security partnerships, no third-party power is currently capable of replacing the United States as the dominant military actor in the Middle East. The military equipment, command structures, logistics systems, and operational networks of Gulf Arab states remain deeply integrated with the United States. Any rapid transition toward alternative suppliers would create substantial disruptions and inefficiencies.
Neither Russia, China, nor Pakistan currently possesses the capacity to fill the strategic vacuum that would emerge if U.S. security commitments were substantially reduced. Consequently, while some Gulf Arab states may reassess their relationship with Washington, such reassessments are more likely to produce strategic adjustments than a fundamental rupture.
articles.summary: The war is also creating strategic opportunities for Washington and new challenges for Beijing in the Middle East.

articles.title: China’s Asian Affairs Reshuffle
articles.full_text:
The elevation of a former ambassador to Mongolia signals a shift in diplomatic execution – but the change can only go so far.
Mongolian President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa receives then-Chinese Ambassador Shen Minjuan and awards her the Order of the Polar State, Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, July 22, 2026.
On July 21, President Khurelsukh Ukhnaa awarded Shen Minjuan, China’s ambassador to the country since 2023, Mongolia’s Order of the Polar Star (Altangadas), the country’s highest state honor for foreign nationals. Barely a week later, on July 29, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) updated its official organizational roster: Shen had taken office as director-general of the Department of Asian Affairs, succeeding Liu Jinsong. 
The speed of the promotion was striking. So was its symbolism. For Mongolian policymakers and analysts who observed Shen’s nearly three-year tenure up close, her elevation to one of the most influential operational posts in Chinese foreign policy is more than a routine bureaucratic rotation. It is the clearest signal yet that Beijing is recalibrating its approach to its immediate periphery – moving away from the overtly assertive style that defined much of the past half-decade toward a more calibrated, geoeconomics-driven model.
From a Mongolian vantage point, this adjustment makes eminent strategic sense for China. Years of so-called “wolf warrior diplomacy” have yielded diminishing returns across its neighborhood. A more unyielding diplomatic approach accelerated hedging behavior in Southeast Asia, deepened security coordination between Washington and its regional allies, and made it harder for smaller states to maintain the balanced, pragmatic relations most prefer. 
Shen’s record in Ulaanbaatar suggests she understands this dynamic. Her task now is to apply lessons learned in a relatively manageable bilateral setting to a vastly more complex regional portfolio. The vacancy she leaves behind in Mongolia – and who fills it – will offer an early clue as to how broadly this new approach is intended to apply.
This recalibration has precedents. China’s neighborhood diplomacy has cycled between more assertive and more cooperative modes roughly every five to seven years, most notably after the 2013 Neighborhood Diplomacy Work Conference and again after the 2018 and 2025 rounds of tightening U.S. strategic competition.
To grasp the significance of the reshuffle, one must first assess the tenure of Liu Jinsong, who led the Department of Asian Affairs from 2021 through mid-2026. A career diplomat with postings across Japan, India, Afghanistan, and the United Kingdom, Liu brought firm diplomatic instincts to the role. His tenure coincided with a period of intensifying regional friction, and his approach prioritized clear deterrence signaling, rigid line-drawing on sovereignty issues, and public displays of resolve – a tone that resonated with domestic nationalist audiences in China but generated mounting pushback across the region.
The most widely noted episode came in November 2025, during bilateral consultations with Kanai Masaaki, director-general of Japan’s Asian and Oceanian Affairs Bureau. The meeting followed a diplomatic firestorm triggered by Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s parliamentary remarks framing a potential Taiwan contingency as an existential security threat to Japan. Photographs from the encounter showed Liu delivering China’s formal protest with his hands tucked into his trouser pockets, gaze directed downward toward his counterpart. The image, which circulated widely across regional media, was interpreted in many capitals as a deliberate display of both dominance and displeasure.
In Ulaanbaatar, such episodes are watched with a mixture of detachment and quiet concern. Mongolia has no direct stake in the East China Sea or South China Sea disputes, but the broader pattern of Chinese diplomatic posture matters a great deal. When Beijing leans heavily on public confrontation and hierarchical signaling, smaller states across the region tend to accelerate their diversification efforts. For Mongolia, this dynamic reinforces the logic of the Third Neighbor policy – the country’s longstanding strategy of cultivating ties with the United States, Japan, the European Union, South Korea, and Turkiye to balance its dependence on China and Russia.
Liu’s approach, while fully consistent with Beijing’s non-negotiable positions on Taiwan and territorial integrity, contributed to a regional atmosphere in which multivector balancing became the default posture for many capitals. Reports that Liu may be reassigned as China’s next ambassador to Australia fit a clear logic of matching diplomatic temperament to theater. Rather than repudiating Liu’s approach, China is aiming it at a different target. In a bilateral relationship defined by deep structural distrust, AUKUS-driven security frictions, and values-based divergences, a firm, unyielding envoy remains a fitting instrument. 
But for China’s immediate backyard, where economic interdependence runs far deeper and smaller states actively resist binary geopolitical choices, a different operational tone is now required. That is where Shen Minjuan comes in.
Shen’s record as China’s ambassador to Mongolia offers a window into the diplomatic model she is likely to bring to her broader regional portfolio. She arrived in Ulaanbaatar in October 2023 with prior postings in Malaysia and Indonesia and experience as deputy director-general for Southeast Asian affairs. Both professionally and educationally – Shen holds a master’s degree in economics – her background is shaped far more by trade, investment, and consensus-building than by security confrontation.
In Mongolia, her approach prioritized practical deliverables over public confrontation. The long-delayed Gashuun Sukhait-Gants Mod cross-border railway, a critical artery for Mongolia’s mineral exports that had languished in negotiations for nearly two decades, moved from planning into active construction during her watch. Today, it’s on track for a 2027 commissioning. Bilateral trade progressed steadily toward the $20 billion target set by both national leaders. Energy and infrastructure cooperation advanced steadily, including upstream oil projects positioned to supply Mongolia’s first domestic refinery in Altanshiree soum, Dornogobi province. Targeted humanitarian assistance during severe winter dzud disasters reinforced working relationships across the Mongolian political spectrum, and high-level exchanges remained consistent and constructive.
Crucially, these outcomes did not require Mongolia to abandon its Third Neighbor orientation. Diversification continued, as it must for a landlocked democracy situated between two major powers. Shen did not attempt to force Mongolia to make a binary choice.
But Shen never abandoned China’s red lines, either. Taiwanese media reports from October 2024 alleged that the Chinese Embassy had pressed local authorities to restrict Taiwan’s Double Tenth reception and had limited foreign diplomats’ access to a Jetsun Dampa-related event at Gandan Monastery. These claims, while consistent with Beijing’s longstanding insistence on the One China principle, remain primarily sourced from Taiwanese outlets and lack independent official confirmation from Mongolian authorities. They nonetheless underscore a broader reality. Shen demonstrated that firmness on Chinese core interests – particularly regarding Taiwan and related sovereignty sensitivities – could coexist with steady progress on economic complementarity.
From a Mongolian perspective, this combination proved workable. It reduced unnecessary friction without compromising the fundamental strategic autonomy that Ulaanbaatar seeks to preserve. Critically, this model is not a retreat from Chinese interests; it is a more sophisticated tool for advancing them. By frontloading economic gains, Beijing lowers the domestic political cost for Mongolian leaders to accommodate its preferences, while raising the implicit price of deviation from its core red lines. 
Scholarly observers have noted, however, that this transactional focus carries long-term trade-offs: prioritizing infrastructure and commodity deliverables over deeper societal, educational, and cultural exchange risks narrowing the bilateral relationship to a purely economic bargain, eroding the reservoir of public goodwill that underpins strategic trust.
Shen now inherits a portfolio of deep-seated structural problems that extend far beyond the Sino-Mongolian relationship, and that no change in personnel can fully resolve. The South China Sea remains the most volatile flashpoint. China and the Philippines have seen repeated standoffs under the Ferdinand Marcos Jr. administration, which is backed by expanding minilateral naval coordination among the United States, Japan, and Australia. China-Japan relations remain in a deep freeze, with Japan’s ongoing defense expansion and deepened security partnerships presenting formidable structural barriers. The China-India border stalemate persists; despite a recent thaw in the overall relationship, New Delhi continues to solidify border infrastructure and deepen Quad engagement. Finally, the Korean Peninsula continues to generate instability, with North Korea’s advancing nuclear programs and deepening alignment with Russia limiting Beijing’s room for maneuver.
The central test of Shen’s tenure is whether the Mongolia model can scale to China’s broader neighborhood diplomacy – and there are strong reasons for skepticism. Mongolia was a relatively manageable case: it shares a stable, long-demarcated border with China; its economy is structurally dependent on Chinese markets and infrastructure; and its Third Neighbor policy is designed to complement rather than confront Chinese regional influence. In that environment, prioritizing economic deliverables and de-escalating public friction is a low-risk, high-reward strategy.
The same logic does not apply cleanly to the South China Sea, the East China Sea, or the Sino-Indian border, where partners maintain active security alliances with the United States, hold competing territorial claims, and face strong domestic nationalist incentives to push back. Economic statecraft can raise the cost of confrontation, but it cannot offset security-driven hedging – and in some cases, it is perceived as economic coercion, further hardening positions. At best, Shen may succeed in lowering the temperature of regional diplomacy.
It is also important to delineate the boundaries of Shen’s authority. As director-general of Asian Affairs, she influences bureaucratic sequencing, tone management, and the prioritization of functional cooperation. She does not set strategic direction. Core decisions on sovereignty thresholds, Taiwan policy, and responses to U.S. alliance architecture are made at the level of the Central Foreign Affairs Commission, not the by a Foreign Ministry department. Shen’s promotion therefore signals an adjustment in execution style: greater reliance on geoeconomic inducements and quiet diplomacy to advance the same set of core interests. This is a tactical calibration, not a strategic rewrite.
Shen also faces internal constraints on her ability to shift tone. Domestic nationalist public opinion in China acts as a de facto floor on diplomatic flexibility, and perceived softness on sovereignty reliably triggers backlash. She must also coordinate across bureaucratic silos – the Ministry of Commerce, border control agencies, and the military – each with its own institutional priorities. Most fundamentally, the broader context of China-U.S. strategic competition has not changed. As long as Washington deepens its regional alliance architecture, Beijing will continue to prioritize deterrence, regardless of diplomatic style.
Shen Minjuan’s ascent to lead China’s Department of Asian Affairs is best understood not as a dramatic policy reversal, but as a deliberate upgrading of Beijing’s diplomatic execution. Her tenure in Mongolia provided a proof of concept: that calibrated, economically focused engagement can advance Chinese interests while containing nationalist backlash and preserving working relationships with a neighbor actively pursuing external diversification. Whether that model can be scaled across a far more complex and contested regional landscape remains to be seen.
For Mongolia, the immediate takeaway is one of cautious opportunity. The forthcoming ambassadorial appointment to Ulaanbaatar will provide an early signal of how broadly this new diplomatic playbook will be applied. If Beijing selects another pragmatic, project-focused envoy drawn from the standard Asian Affairs pipeline, it will suggest that Shen’s approach is being institutionalized as transferable practice. A more security- or ideology-focused appointee, by contrast, would indicate that the recalibration is limited in scope.
For Mongolia and other small regional states, the prudent response is cautious pragmatism, not over-optimism. Shen’s promotion creates a window for lower-friction cooperation, faster project delivery, and more predictable bilateral relations. That is a meaningful gain, and one that Ulaanbaatar should seize. But it would be a mistake to read a fundamental strategic shift into a bureaucratic personnel change. China’s core regional objectives – securing its borders, consolidating economic centrality, and limiting external military presence in its neighborhood – remain constant. What changes is the mix of tools used to pursue them.
Personnel changes do not rewrite geopolitical realities, but they fundamentally shape how those realities are managed. In placing a technically fluent, relationship-focused operator at the helm of its Asian affairs, Beijing has signaled that in the long competition for Asia’s future, tactical sophistication may be one of the more underrated instruments of national power. For neighbors like Mongolia, the task is to navigate this recalibrated landscape with eyes open: seizing opportunities for practical cooperation while safeguarding the strategic autonomy that has long defined the country’s foreign policy identity.

articles.title: Hopes for the North Korean Human Rights Act of 2026
articles.full_text:
The North Korean Human Rights Act of 2004 expired in 2022. An important bipartisan effort seeks to reauthorize it.
Since the COVID-19 border closures sealed North Korea off from the world, and as the China-Russia-North Korea axis has deepened, the North Korean people have become more isolated and vulnerable than at any point in recent memory. In this grim period, one piece of encouraging news stands out: last month, U.S. Senators Tim Kaine (D-VA) and Dan Sullivan (R-AK) introduced the bipartisan North Korean Human Rights Reauthorization Act (NKHRA).
Growing up in North Korea, America was my enemy – alongside South Korea, the U.S. is one of the two principal adversaries the state taught us to despise. I was taught that American missionaries had pressed the word “thief” into an innocent boy’s forehead with caustic acid. We called Americans “wolf-like Yankee imperialists” and were told they sought to swallow the Korean peninsula whole. 
When I escaped in 2013, I carried that conditioning with me – until American volunteers with no family ties to North Korea, no personal stake, no obligation, wept and prayed alongside me for the family I had left behind. And as I slowly learned the truth about the outside world, I discovered something that humbled me entirely: the very government I had been raised to fear had passed the North Korean Human Rights Act in 2004, becoming the first country in the world to formally recognize that what was happening inside North Korea was not merely a political problem, but ongoing crimes against humanity. The Americans had been fighting for people they would never meet, in a country they were prohibited from entering, for decades.
The North Korean Human Rights Act, or NKHRA, expired in 2022.
On June 25, Senators Kane and Sullivan reintroduced the NKHRA, signaling Congress’s continued commitment to advancing the rights of the North Korean people. This effort to revive the NKHRA legislation is part of a long bipartisan tradition. In the House of Representatives, Representative Young Kim (R-CA) and many others have worked persistently to reauthorize the NKHRA . And as a congressional staffer explained during a meeting at this year’s North Korean Young Leaders Assembly (NKYLA), the gap since 2022 has not reflected a lack of American commitment to North Korean human rights – the tenure of Special Envoy Julie Turner from 2023 to 2025 demonstrated that clearly – but rather is a matter of timing between the legislative and executive branches. The commitment has endured; the legal architecture must now be restored. 
The 2025 update to the U.N. Commission of Inquiry on Human Rights in the DPRK confirmed that conditions inside North Korea have deteriorated sharply. Consuming foreign media can now result in public execution. Political prison camps continue to hold tens of thousands under conditions amounting to ongoing crimes against humanity. The deepening alignment of China’s Xi Jinping, Russia’s Vladimir Putin, and North Korea’s Kim Jong Un has further shielded the regime from international accountability – and as that axis tightens, the window for outside engagement with the North Korean people grows narrower.
Reauthorizing the NKHRA is the right first step. But it should be accompanied by meaningful action across several fronts. 
First, the NKHRA should expand support for information access. A single piece of outside information can dismantle years of state indoctrination. As North Korea’s isolation deepens, the quality of information reaching its people matters as much as the quantity. Future efforts should prioritize substantive content that helps ordinary North Koreans understand the failures of their own political, economic, and social systems – equipping them not only to question what they have been told, but to envision what a different Korea could look like. 
Second, the United States and South Korea should simultaneously appoint special envoys for North Korean human rights – positions that have both sat vacant for years. The previous pairing of U.S. Special Envoy Julie Turner and South Korean Special Envoy Lee Shin-wha demonstrated what coordinated bilateral engagement can achieve. That synergy must be restored.
Third, young North Korean defectors, such as members of NKYLA – now professionals, researchers, lawyers, and civic leaders in democratic societies – must be brought into the policy process as genuine partners, not symbolic witnesses. 
Finally, the forced repatriation of North Korean refugees in China must remain a central concern of international human rights diplomacy. Every North Korean returned to the regime faces severe punishment – often imprisonment or death. Greater international attention and explicit provisions in the reauthorized Act can raise the diplomatic cost for China of continuing this practice. 
America was the first country to legislate on behalf of the North Korean people. It did so not because North Koreans asked but because the United States chose to see our humanity when our own government denied it. To the senators, representatives, and American citizens who have sustained this commitment across more than two decades: on behalf of those who cannot yet speak for themselves, thank you. The North Korean people see what you have done, even when they cannot thank you themselves.

Since the COVID-19 border closures sealed North Korea off from the world, and as the China-Russia-North Korea axis has deepened, the North Korean people have become more isolated and vulnerable than at any point in recent memory. In this grim period, one piece of encouraging news stands out: last month, U.S. Senators Tim Kaine (D-VA) and Dan Sullivan (R-AK) introduced the bipartisan North Korean Human Rights Reauthorization Act (NKHRA).
Growing up in North Korea, America was my enemy – alongside South Korea, the U.S. is one of the two principal adversaries the state taught us to despise. I was taught that American missionaries had pressed the word “thief” into an innocent boy’s forehead with caustic acid. We called Americans “wolf-like Yankee imperialists” and were told they sought to swallow the Korean peninsula whole. 
Eunsook Jang holds a bachelor’s degree in political science from Korea University and a master’s degree in international development from Brandeis University. A Fulbright Scholar and North Korean defector, she is currently a research intern at a leading think tank in Washington, D.C., where her work focuses on human rights in Asia, North Korean and Asia-Pacific policy development, and post-reunification development planning for the Korean Peninsula.
articles.summary: The North Korean Human Rights Act of 2004 expired in 2022. An important bipartisan effort seeks to reauthorize it.

articles.title: India’s Climate Stress and the Solar Power Paradox
articles.full_text:

This trend has continued unabated into subsequent months, with high temperatures and humidity levels driving increased use of cooling appliances such as air conditioners across many states in India.
