The peak power demand also jumped to 270.20 GW in July 2026. It was 220.74 GW in July 2025. The all-time record high was set in May this year with demand of 270.82 GW. 
The steep rise in temperature and heat waves may be a problem for people, but for the leading air conditioner manufacturers, it is a buoyant market. Companies like Voltas and LG Electronics have reported high sales. Each had already sold over 1 million units in the first three months of the year. Panasonic India said its residential AC sales increased by 50 percent year-on-year in the summer season of 2026, representing its highest-ever level. 
These are very high figures for a developing country, where 60 percent of the population depends on food subsidies and power bills are on a constant rise. It also demonstrates the fact that the rising middle class, not just in metros, but also in tier-two towns and beyond, is responding to the threat and discomfort of a warming climate with significant uptake of household cooling options. Access to air conditioning, seen increasingly as a significant health issue globally, also contributes to the global warming and climate crisis. 
According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), global electricity demand is expected to grow by 3.6 percent in 2026 and 3.8 percent in 2027, driven by industry, cooling, electric vehicles (EVs), and data centers. In India, one of the world’s fastest-growing major electricity markets, it is projected to grow at 7 percent,  twice the global average. In comparison, it will grow at 5.5 percent in China, 1.8 percent in the U.S., and 2.1 percent in Europe. 
El Niño, a climate pattern in which surface waters in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean become significantly warmer than average, is projected to turbocharge extreme weather across the planet this year. India is already witnessing a deficient monsoon in 2026, attributable to the El Niño underway. According to the India Meteorological Department (IMD) and government vulnerability assessments, the country’s central, eastern, and northeastern regions face the highest drought risks. Reports have already indicated its possible impact on electricity generation. States like Odisha are considering a halt in hydropower generation to prioritize drinking water and irrigation. The southern states of Karnataka is prioritizing drinking water over irrigation for agriculture. 
However, even with the ongoing war in Iran – which has created enormous hurdles for energy imports for India – the country has managed to generate enough power to meet this rise in demand. While international energy prices have risen during the first half of the year, India’s wholesale electricity spot prices declined by around 10 percent.  This would not have been possible without India’s perennial and increasing reliance on coal, which provides 74 percent of the total power generation. 
There has been a steady growth in solar energy generation as well, under the government’s Solar Parks Scheme. Official data by India’s Ministry of New and Renewable Energy indicated that solar energy generation has surged nearly 138 percent over a four-year period, rising from 73.48 BU in 2021- 22 to 174.76 BU in 2025- 26. Currently, solar energy supplies more than 60 GW, around 22 percent of India’s daytime peak electricity demand, highlighting its growing role in meeting rising consumption. 
At the same time, however, the initiative has faced major challenges turning such massive solar capacity into stable power. Billions of units of electricity continue to be wasted because the grid cannot absorb massive surges during peak sunshine hours. Transmission lines lag behind solar park construction, leaving tens of gigawatts of capacity underutilized or on temporary connections. Moreover, coal generators struggle to reduce output quickly during peak solar production without incurring costly and lengthy shutdowns, leading to wasted solar energy on the grid.
India’s chronic pollution problem poses additional challenges. A recent study indicated that in India, aerosols in the air have reduced the amount of solar power generated by 9.6 percent in 2023, equivalent to around 15 terawatt-hours (TWh). The global average loss due to the same cause in 2023 was 5.8 percent.  Between 2017 and 2023, pollution-related electricity generation losses from existing installations averaged 74 TWh a year, which is roughly one third of the electricity generated every year by new solar capacity. India’s loss is one of the world’s highest.
The core challenge facing the country is no longer just building solar panels, but managing grid integration, storage shortages, and transmission bottlenecks that force widespread power curtailment. India’s current operational energy storage capacity includes roughly 6 GW to 7.5 GW of pumped storage hydro projects (PSPs) and over 1 GWh to 7.5 GWh of operational battery energy storage systems (BESS), which are grossly inadequate. In comparison, China’s operational non-conventional energy storage capacity reached roughly 153 GW in mid-2026. All this explains India’s continued reliance on coal-driven thermal power generation.
At one level, these can be considered expected transition problems. China, the world’s largest producer of solar energy, for example, went through a similar transition problem between 2011 and 2016, when it built wind and solar capacity far faster than it built the grid infrastructure to move that power around. Meanwhile, heat waves and demand spikes will arise regardless of infrastructure readiness. articles.title: No Wonderland: Alice’s Shameful Australian Aboriginal Camps
articles.full_text:
The conditions in and around Australia’s Aboriginal camps, such as the one where a 5-year-old girl was murdered in April, are shameful for one of the world’s wealthiest countries.
Alice Springs, or “Alice” as it is commonly known here in Australia, is situated in the country’s Red Center. For over 30,000 years, the Arrernte Aboriginal people have been custodians of this remote land – a land of red earth, awe-inspiring rock formations and ethereal skies. 
Alice, or Mparntwe in the Arrernte language, has profound, unhealed wounds, both ancient and recent. The most recent, and still painfully raw, is the murder in late April of a 5-year-old girl. An Aboriginal man by the name of Jefferson Lewis has been charged with her murder. 
In accordance with Aboriginal custom, under which the names of the dead are avoided out of respect, the family requested she be called Kumanjayi Little Baby. She was found dead after disappearing from the Aboriginal Old Timers Camp, one of the 18 Aboriginal camps on the fringes of Alice Springs. 
Kumanjayi Little Baby’s family were staying in a dilapidated house at the Old Timers Camp after traveling from their remote community in the Tanami Desert to Alice Springs to access medical care. Photos taken at the Old Timers Camp during the search for the girl showed a mattress on the floor where she had been put to bed before her disappearance. 
Police said Jefferson Lewis, the alleged killer of Kumanjayi Little Baby, was staying at the Old Timers Camp too. A May editorial in The Sydney Morning Herald hit the nail on the head about the tragedy, describing the camps as “gathering places for the powerless and the outcast, where the most vulnerable are easy prey, and protections are minimal.” 
Senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price, who is also the aunt of Kumanjayi Little Baby, said, “Too many [camps] have become environments where safety is not guaranteed, particularly for children.” She added that “for too long, there has been a reluctance to speak plainly about the conditions in and around town camps.”
The conditions in and around the Aboriginal camps, not only in Alice Springs but all over Australia, are shameful for one of the world’s wealthiest countries. After all, it is, as Australian writer and academic Donald Horne called it, the “Lucky Country.”
In this “Lucky Country,” Aboriginal people remain Australia’s unlucky first inhabitants. In remote regions, especially, they face hardships more often associated with poorer nations: poverty, health inequities, high incarceration rates, inadequate housing, violence – the dreadful list goes on. If there’s a place in Australia where the struggles faced by Aboriginal communities are most vividly felt, it must be the camps. 
In the bureaucratic banal parlance, the camps are called: “Alice Springs Community Living Areas.” In the camps, there is nothing that resembles community living; let’s be fair dinkum – using a traditional Aussie expression. 
According to a 2025 report by the Menzies School of Health Research, there are approximately 4,000 residents across the Alice Springs camps. Conditions at many camps are poor, with limited services and shared residences among extended family members. Overcrowding is chronic. The number of residents can almost double during major events like the football carnival and the Alice Springs Show, straining already stretched housing stock.
“Overcrowding and poor-quality housing are associated with poor health, educational and employment outcomes, and increased family violence,” concluded a 2022 report by the Australian National Audit Office. “The highest levels of overcrowding occur in remote areas of the Northern Territory.”
Residents report delays regarding repairs and maintenance. When infrastructure breaks down – bore water lines, roofing, essential utilities – residents often struggle to get timely fixes because it is genuinely unclear which agency is responsible.
The governance of the camps is fragmented. Tangentyere Council Aboriginal Corporation, comprising 15 housing associations, manages the town camps and is responsible for their social and infrastructure services.
Residents say the flow of money and the division of responsibilities are opaque and frustrating. “Current governance arrangements in the Indigenous housing system are complex and poorly coordinated,” said a 2026 study by the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute.
Ken Marchingo, chief executive of Community Housing Central Australia (CHCA), stated that there were too many points of intersection in camp management and that a single responsible organization could clarify accountability.
Many residents and advocates argue that the 2007 “Intervention” has worsened conditions. The 2007 Northern Territory Intervention, officially known as the Northern Territory National Emergency Response, has been criticized for overriding self-determination and for imposing discriminatory, top-down control.
Local organizations, including Tangentyere Council and Community Housing Central Australia, have spent more than a decade developing a proposal to return management of the town camps to the community. They argued that community control would provide clearer accountability and more responsive services.
Many of the camps rely heavily on one-off government grants to get by, and changes to their governance were recommended as far back as 2017. Executive director of township leasing, Pennie Weadon, said her team had repeatedly recommended to the Northern Territory government ways to improve economic opportunities in the camps.
The camps were established in the 1880s, with the arrival of Europeans in Central Australia. Located across the plains and on the outskirts of Alice Springs, they were set up in response to racist policies that banned Aboriginal people, displaced from their lands, from entering the town itself. Between 1928 and 1964, the whole of Alice Springs was a prohibited area for Aboriginal people between sunset and sunrise.
“The town campers, or fringe dwellers as these people were called, were regarded as a problem for the township and much time,” wrote researchers Michael Heppell and Julian J. Wigley in their 1981 monograph about the establishment and development of Alice’s camps. “For decades, Aborigines in Alice Springs were little more than creatures of the authorities, being pushed here and there to suit the whims of some particular administrator or petty official.”
“Welcome to rainy Alice,” the receptionist at my hotel in Alice Springs greeted me. After a steady and unexpected spell of rain, the red earth of Australia’s Red Center is now covered by green grass. It is not the welcome green grass, though. It is buffelgrass, one of the gravest environmental threats to Australia’s arid rangelands.
The flowers at the entrance to the Old Timers Camp – where Kumanjayi Little Baby was abducted last April – have withered. The scars of her murder remain fresh, though. Her solitude on a floor sleeping mattress in the Old Timers Camp and her subsequent murder have once again awakened Australians’ consciousness. No wonderland in the Aboriginal town camps of Alice Springs – just sorrow. And intolerable shame.

articles.title: Taiwan’s Missing Deterrent
articles.full_text:
Conventional deterrence alone overlooks the vector of conflict most likely to define a cross-strait crisis: civil defense.
A scene from Taipei’s 2025 Urban Resilience Exercise, the civil defense portion of the Han Kuang exercise, July 17, 2025.
Deterrence has been a consistent national priority for Taiwan amid the intensifying pressure from China, which frames reunification with Taiwan as an essential component to the Chinese Communist Party’s goal of national rejuvenation, nominally targeted for 2049. Taiwan’s deterrence strategy relies heavily on U.S. arms sales, security assistance, and military technology cooperation.
Conventional deterrents are necessary: F-16V fighters, Indigenous Defense Fighters, and Patriot missile systems prevent adversarial air superiority; Hsiung Feng anti-ship missiles, sea mines, and Harpoon Coastal Defense Systems repel amphibious invasions; ground forces and HIMARS batteries help blunt, endure, and counter an initial attack. Conventional capabilities are acquired and designed to make military advances prohibitively costly for China. 
However, conventional deterrence alone overlooks the vector of conflict most likely to define a cross-strait crisis: civil defense. Chinese tactics in economic coercion are well-documented, Taiwan’s submarine cable network remains vulnerable to sabotage, and Beijing maintains a cognitive warfare apparatus designed to disinform and manipulate Taiwanese public opinion. These challenges cannot be dealt with purely militarily; they require robust civil defense that resists unconventional ruptures to the continuity of life and develops societal preparedness to withstand crises.
The establishment of the All-Out Defense Mobilization Agency, the introduction of “whole-of-society resilience” in official rhetoric, and civilian resources pointed at a military invasion illustrate how civil defense is prioritized within Taiwan’s defense strategy. Yet, Taiwan’s current civil defense capabilities remain insufficient due to fragmented preparedness initiatives, uneven civil-military coordination, and domestic political stagnation.
Today, protracted conflicts necessitate building resilient civil defense capabilities to withstand technologically superior adversaries. Ukraine’s sustained resistance to Russia’s invasion demonstrates that credible civil defense raises the cost of war for the aggressor and complicates an adversary’s expectation of quick and decisive victory. Learning from the Russia-Ukraine War and South Korea, Taiwan can apply their logic to its unique geography and threat profile to raise the cost of coercion and deny Beijing’s expectations of a swift conflict, kinetic or otherwise. 
Civil society organizations currently drive much of the civil defense activity within Taiwan. Groups like Kuma Academy and Forward Alliance train citizens in evacuation planning, open-source intelligence techniques to counter disinformation campaigns, and first aid. The aim is to prepare civilians to respond to kinetic conflict, with courses on causality care and supply reserves, while also increasing public awareness of provocative actions under the threshold of war – gray zone activity – against Taiwan. While still new, these groups have grown quickly: Forward Alliance’s waitlist grew past 1,000 people shortly after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and both organizations saw sustained demand amid consistent Chinese military exercise near the island, indicating growing support within Taiwan’s own populace to advance such initiatives. 
However, these efforts operate largely apart from government funding and integration. A major source of funding for Kuma Academy, for example, has been private philanthropy, with over US$31 million donated by businessman Robert Tsao in 2022. Taipei has pledged a “whole-of-society” defense approach, a framework that seeks to integrate government and civil-society capacity across five areas: civilian training, strategic material stockpiling, critical infrastructure, social welfare and evacuation readiness, and communications network security. Taiwan’s leaders are concerned about China’s ability to disrupt the island’s internal and external communications systems and internet connectivity, emphasizing the importance of a strong, preemptive civil-military coordination.
Taiwan already maintains a comprehensive legal framework for civilian defense in the Civil Defense Act, enacted in 2001 and last amended in 2021; the issue lies in implementation. Under Article 2, the law establishes a nationwide civil defense structure, ranging from municipal to village-level units, with special corps for critical infrastructure and mandating training in evacuation, disaster rescue, and support of military tasks. However, legislative review indicates only between 2 and 13 percent of local civil defense budgets are earmarked for tactical training. Taiwan also has an extensive shelter network; yet a lack of accessibility, maintenance, and emergency provisions bring into question their wartime utility. 
Civil defense reform is also stalled by domestic partisan division. The ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) has moved to formalize resilience efforts, but the opposition Kuomintang (KMT) has protested these efforts as “militarization” of daily life, stalling progress. 
South Korea, which resumed its annual large-scale civil defense drills in 2023 after a six-year hiatus, illustrates how civil defense can be institutionalized for civilian populations. The country uses an all-hazards resilience framing based on the Framework Act on the Management of Disasters and Safety; it does not explicitly set preparedness in the context of wartime contingencies. Certain competencies, such as evacuation planning and critical infrastructure protocols, are readily transferable from disaster management to conflict scenarios.
South Korea also maintains a Civil Defense Corps, comprising men aged 20 to 40, who have completed their mandatory military service. Required hours of training scale down based on years of service. The Civil Defense Corps maintains the dual function structure: in wartime, reservists are trained to guide evacuations, conduct rescue operations, and respond to biological and chemical accidents; in peacetime, they assist in disaster response that entail similar protocols. This model provides consistent exposure to citizens that institutionalizes civil defense in a low-stakes environment while normalizing procedures in public consciousness.
Taiwan can also learn from civil defense challenges in South Korea. For one, Seoul only announced plans for its first CBRN-resistant bunkers in 2025, targeting 2028 completion. That means current shelter infrastructure does not match the adversary’s offensive capabilities. Also, the South Korean populace regularly neglects civil defense drills because many lack the perception of an imminent threat, namely from North Korea. That gap both hampers societal preparedness and creates dissonance between civilians and government leadership.
To counter public indifference to civil defense, South Korea has raised the perceived stakes and lowered the friction of engagement. The Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise in 2022, with cooperation from the United States, unfolded alongside the Ulchi government-level disaster preparedness drills. The combination grounded civilian training in a visibly serious military drill, a contrast to the public announcements to take shelter and clear the roads that characterize standard civil defense practices. The Korean Public Alert System, further, provides an easy access point for emergency updates and is pre-installed to commercial smartphones. 
Notably, South Korea has fundamental differences from Taiwan that re-emphasize the importance of credible civil defense. Having a physical border with its primary adversary and the Korean War stalemate necessitated and initially embedded robust civil defense infrastructure into society. Unlike Taiwan, South Korea enjoys a mandated military defense commitment from the United States. Without parallel safeguards, Taiwan’s island geography necessitates contingency plans for its vulnerable communications with an exceptional shelter network and strategic reserves for potential blockades.
Learning from South Korea, Taiwan has an actionable path toward upgrading its civil defense to match the Civil Defense Act mandate.
Taiwan can curate its annually published handbook with emphasis on dual-use framing between natural disasters and military operations, partially alleviating the risk of partisan accusations. Anticipated typhoons and potential Chinese aggression both necessitate backup power, mobile generators, and redundant communication systems. Further focus on general disaster preparedness and the transferable competencies creates a civilian resource that has high utility given Taiwan’s high vulnerability to natural disasters while being more difficult to scrutinize for politically hedging rhetoric.
Taiwan’s civil preparedness could also benefit from increased transparency on civil defense fund spending. A minimum percent expenditure on civilian training, for instance, could ensure that civil defense budgets are not squandered on social events. Furthermore, while faithful execution depends on local governments, a clearer, apolitical natural disaster framework that subtly prioritizes overlapping skillsets could assuage an expected political dissent.
Most potent is the potential for institutionalized coordination between the All-Out Defense Mobilization Agency and established civil society organizations. Taiwan could extend training capacity, plus giving these groups defined roles within the “whole-of-society resilience” framework could bolster disaster preparedness without leaving them to operate in parallel. Extending the disaster curriculums of organizations like Kuma Academy alongside a rapid communication network like South Korea’s public alert system could further broaden the reach beyond dedicated volunteers. 
Public opinion polling revealed that 65.6 percent of respondents believe civil-military interactions during disaster relief improves their impression of the military while 64 percent called natural disaster a serious national threat, a slight increase from the 55 percent who directly cite China. Taken together, these findings indicate that an approach that emphasizes the natural disaster elements to civil defense is unlikely to be read as overtly militaristic while ensuring the island is prepared and resilient for any challenges it may face.

Ukraine’s sustained resistance to Russia’s invasion demonstrates that credible civil defense raises the cost of war for the aggressor and complicates an adversary’s expectation of quick and decisive victory. Learning from the Russia-Ukraine War and South Korea, Taiwan can apply their logic to its unique geography and threat profile to raise the cost of coercion and deny Beijing’s expectations of a swift conflict, kinetic or otherwise. 
Civil society organizations currently drive much of the civil defense activity within Taiwan. Groups like Kuma Academy and Forward Alliance train citizens in evacuation planning, open-source intelligence techniques to counter disinformation campaigns, and first aid. The aim is to prepare civilians to respond to kinetic conflict, with courses on causality care and supply reserves, while also increasing public awareness of provocative actions under the threshold of war – gray zone activity – against Taiwan. While still new, these groups have grown quickly: Forward Alliance’s waitlist grew past 1,000 people shortly after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and both organizations saw sustained demand amid consistent Chinese military exercise near the island, indicating growing support within Taiwan’s own populace to advance such initiatives. 
However, these efforts operate largely apart from government funding and integration. A major source of funding for Kuma Academy, for example, has been private philanthropy, with over US$31 million donated by businessman Robert Tsao in 2022. Taipei has pledged a “whole-of-society” defense approach, a framework that seeks to integrate government and civil-society capacity across five areas: civilian training, strategic material stockpiling, critical infrastructure, social welfare and evacuation readiness, and communications network security. Taiwan’s leaders are concerned about China’s ability to disrupt the island’s internal and external communications systems and internet connectivity, emphasizing the importance of a strong, preemptive civil-military coordination.
Taiwan already maintains a comprehensive legal framework for civilian defense in the Civil Defense Act, enacted in 2001 and last amended in 2021; the issue lies in implementation. Under Article 2, the law establishes a nationwide civil defense structure, ranging from municipal to village-level units, with special corps for critical infrastructure and mandating training in evacuation, disaster rescue, and support of military tasks. However, legislative review indicates only between 2 and 13 percent of local civil defense budgets are earmarked for tactical training. Taiwan also has an extensive shelter network; yet a lack of accessibility, maintenance, and emergency provisions bring into question their wartime utility. 
Civil defense reform is also stalled by domestic partisan division. The ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) has moved to formalize resilience efforts, but the opposition Kuomintang (KMT) has protested these efforts as “militarization” of daily life, stalling progress.
articles.summary: Conventional deterrence alone overlooks the vector of conflict most likely to define a cross-strait crisis: civil defense.

articles.title: China’s Military Is Now Using AI to Plan Strike Operations
articles.full_text:
What does that mean for the future of human control in war – including a war over Taiwan?
PLA aircraft rehearse for China’s military parade, held in Beijing on Sep. 3, 2025.
The People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force now uses an AI system that draws up plans for large-scale strike operations. Instead of being released with great fanfare, the system appeared in a CCTV documentary released in early August to mark the PLA’s 99th anniversary. The system is described as prioritizing targets from a pool of hundreds, coordinating dozens of formations, and assigning tasks to more than 100 tactical units. According to the documentary, it has already been used in multiple missions.
The timing lines up neatly with Xi Jinping’s instruction in late July that the PLA must strengthen the military application of unmanned intelligent technologies and gradually build an intelligent military system. As China has been pursuing this very goal for years, Xi’s remarks are not new. The level of emphasis, however, is high: Beijing wants steady progress toward the modernization goals set for 2027, which marks the 100th anniversary of the PLA’s founding.
The AI system is described to handle a volume of decisions that would otherwise overwhelm human planners as, so goes the argument, traditional calculation methods cannot keep up when large numbers of aircraft and targets move at high speed. This indeed is a fair assessment and is far from being unique to China. 
Unlike autonomous weapon systems, the software does not select and engage targets directly. Its significance lies higher in the command chain. It helps plan air campaigns by recommending how aircraft, electronic warfare assets, and supporting capabilities should be combined before commanders authorize execution. In other words the system is described as a support tool that helps commanders and pilots – but humans remain responsible for the final decisions.
As is often the case with great powers and military AI, there is a catch in China’s posture and the potential operation realities. On the surface, Beijing has long maintained that artificial intelligence should support human judgment rather than replace it. China’s statements on lethal autonomous weapon systems at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons emphasize that AI should support rather than replace human decision-makers.
On the other side of the AI coin, however, the system’s apparent ability to compress hours of complex campaign planning into minutes risks reducing human authority to barely more than a formal rubber stamp, thus creating a sharp tension between China’s diplomatic posture and its operational realities.
Beijing’s logic is understandable. Decision superiority has become an increasingly important determinant of military effectiveness alongside the quality and quantity of platforms and weapons. Compressing the planning cycle allows commanders to adapt faster to changing battlefield conditions and exploit fleeting opportunities. The problem is that even if humans remain formally in control, AI can alter the pace of conflict enough to reshape how that control is exercised.
When planning happens in minutes, the room for independent human assessment shrinks together with the time frame. Even for pre-validated targets the system works with, judging whether it is military or civilian, whether the expected civilian harm is proportionate, and whether the attack is necessary all require time. 
Under high tempo operations, like executing a coordinated air offensive across the Taiwan Strait, the human role can become little more than rapid approval of options the AI has already ranked. Indeed, this may already be happening in Israel’s strikes on Gaza. A source told reporters, “We prepare the targets automatically … We work quickly and there is no time to delve deep into the target.”
Under such circumstances, the risk of automation bias rises. Accountability grows harder to pin down. If a strike based on an AI-generated plan produces unlawful effects, whom does responsibility sit with exactly? With the commander who accepted the plan? Or with those who designed the system that produced it? Ultimately, keeping a human in the loop satisfies diplomatic requirements, but in practice risks reducing commanders to a convenient legal scapegoat for algorithmic failures
These issues carry weight across the Indo-Pacific and beyond. A system built for fast, coordinated campaigns raises the speed at which China could generate and execute complex strike packages in a South China Sea scenario, for example. Crisis management tools like direct military hotlines or diplomatic signaling that depend on slower human judgment and dialogue may well end up lagging dangerously behind. Consequently, countries in AUKUS and the Quad can no longer rely on traditional de-escalation but must build defense strategies capable of absorbing and countering potential algorithmic shocks.
These strategic implications are far reaching and the system offers a revealing glimpse into how AI can reshape the conditions under which humans may well be making decisions about the use of force. Meaningful human control requires far more than a formal rule that a person stays in the loop, and all is in the green. It needs interfaces, review steps, and training that still allow real judgment when time is short. Compliance with the law of armed conflict works better when those requirements are built into the system from the beginning rather than added later as a quasi-afterthought.
It is important to highlight that the planning system is far from being an isolated project; it fits a broad Chinese pattern. Recent disclosures span AI integration across logistics, intelligence analysis, and battlefield management, pointing to Beijing’s vision for an end-to-end algorithmic command ecosystem. Viewed together, this strategy maintains human oversight in name while embedding machine speed into every stage of military operations. In effect, the service member remains in the loop not to exercise operational control, but to co-sign the machine’s momentum. 
As systems like this one move from demonstration into regular use, Beijing’s statements about human control are bound to face closer examination. Yet without mechanisms to inspect software or verify decision loops, diplomatic pushback will remain stuck somewhere between meager and nonexistent. Meanwhile the actual, for now hard to assess, quality of oversight that PLA branches install in their planning tools will shape both the character of future operations and the chances for workable rules on military AI globally. 
That is to say, the AI arms race just got an algorithmic nitro boost. As systems like this will inevitably proliferate, the fear of falling behind will drive other nations to field their own AI planners, ensuring that machine-speed warfare becomes the global standard. In this brand new, AI driven era, the ever increasing risk is not just that algorithms might fail, but that humans will no longer have the time or agency to stop them.

articles.title: How China Is Reordering Global Governance From Within
articles.full_text:
Beijing’s June white paper leaves the U.N.-centered architecture intact – but re-interprets the priorities.
On June 17, the State Council Information Office published “More Just and Equitable Global Governance: China’s Principles, Proposals and Actions.” Its most revealing line was also its most conservative: “All countries should firmly uphold the international system with the U.N. at its core, safeguard the international order based on international law, and uphold the basic norms governing international relations underpinned by the purposes and principles of the U.N. Charter, instead of reinventing the wheel.” 
On July 16, 29 governments signed the founding agreement of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO) in Shanghai. The new body, headquartered in China, invokes the United Nations Charter and a “people-centered” approach.
Together, these two events capture Beijing’s method for remaking global governance. Rather than propose a rival constitution, China preserves the institutions and texts of the postwar order while reweighting their principles and creating new, China-led venues to operationalize them. China’s visions stresses sovereign equality, noninterference, state-led development, and negotiated consent gain weight; independent scrutiny, adverse judgment, and claims beyond governmental mediation all recede.
Looking for a “status quo” or a “revisionist” China sets up the wrong binary. As Alastair Iain Johnston argued, there is no single international order that a state accepts or rejects; China takes different positions toward issue-specific orders. Beijing calls this “reform,” and the new white paper shows what it looks like in practice.
China’s President Xi Jinping launched the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Plus meeting in Tianjin on September 1, 2025. Its concept paper identified three deficits: Global South underrepresentation, weakened rules, and institutional ineffectiveness on development and new domains such as artificial intelligence. The paper proposed five principles – sovereign equality, international rule of law, multilateralism, a people-centered approach, and “real results” – while insisting that reform meant neither overturning the existing order nor constructing one outside it.
The initiative draws on older concepts: the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, the “democratization of international relations,” and Xi’s “community with a shared future for humanity.” The June 2026 white paper presented development, security, civilization, and governance – the four subjects of China’s global initiatives – as a “complete action framework” covering material promise, stability, plurality, and institutional direction.
However, a coherence imposed after the fact should not be mistaken for a master plan fixed decades ago. Chinese order-building has been cumulative, experimental, and uneven. Today, those scattered positions now form a doctrine institutionalized through coalitions, organizations, and routines. Along the way, China casts itself not as an insurgent but as a guide to an evolution it presents as inevitable.
China’s argument draws from the U.N. Charter, whose commitments have never sat comfortably together. Article 2 affirms sovereign equality and limits U.N. intervention in essentially domestic matters; the preamble, Article 1, and Article 55 also invoke dignity, human rights, development, and fundamental freedoms. Postwar multilateralism joined a plural society of states to an incomplete society of rights-bearing persons.
Sovereign equality is neither Beijing’s invention nor merely authoritarian self-protection. For smaller states, former colonies, and societies exposed to coercion, it protects against empire, tutelage, and great power privilege. China’s “democracy in international relations” recasts equality as a demand to narrow the gap between legal equality and unequal influence. The emphasis on equality also lets China speak as both a major power and a developing country advocate against inherited hierarchies.
But for China, sovereign equality becomes the primary lens through which every other norm is read. The GGI calls it the “foremost premise” of global governance and links equal participation abroad to noninterference and each government’s right to choose its political system and development path. A principle that shields weaker states externally can then insulate public authority internally.
Two forms of democratization must therefore be separated. Fairer representation can democratize relations among states. Holding governments accountable to the people they rule concerns relations within states. The first does not require weaker scrutiny of power, just as political plurality does not require silence about coercion within borders.
China’s “international rule of law” reveals the same tension. Beijing’s objections to unilateral sanctions, extraterritorial jurisdiction, and selectively applied rules are often well founded. Powerful states have used law to discipline others while reserving exceptions for themselves. Yet a legal order needs authoritative procedures and a willingness to remain bound after consent has been given, even when the result is adverse.
The 2016 South China Sea arbitration is a revealing test case. The tribunal did not decide sovereignty over land; it addressed maritime entitlements, feature status, and conduct under the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea. China said the tribunal exceeded its jurisdiction and violated state consent, and on the award’s 10th anniversary again declared it illegal, null, and void, and without binding force. Annex VII of UNCLOS, however, specifies that refusal to take part in arbitration does not halt proceedings, and awards are final and must be complied with. The question is whether treaty procedures remain binding after a tribunal upholds its jurisdiction and a state rejects that ruling.
Western governments weaken any rule-of-law critique of China when they reserve comparable exceptions for themselves. But inconsistency by others cannot answer the question Beijing leaves open: Can international law constrain a great power when an adverse judgment cuts against what it defines as a core interest?
The GGI calls the people of all nations the “fundamental actors” and ultimate beneficiaries of global governance. Yet Chinese texts understand “people-centeredness” chiefly through peace, development, health, security, technological inclusion, and competent delivery. These are substantive goods; economic and social rights are not lesser rights, though Western governments have often treated them as secondary.
Development, however, does not reduce persons to beneficiaries of governmental performance. The U.N. Declaration on the Right to Development makes the human person its central subject, active participant, and beneficiary and treats all human rights and fundamental freedoms as indivisible. The decisive institutional question is: Who defines the public interest, who participates, and who may challenge a government’s account of success?
The joint communiqué after the May 2026 meeting of the Group of Friends recorded agreement on U.N. centrality, Charter principles, reform, practical cooperation, and protecting and promoting human rights. In accompanying remarks, Foreign Minister Wang Yi offered nine Chinese priorities “for further discussion and consideration,” including a “recalibration” of human rights governance and rejection of “human rights above sovereignty.” Those were Chinese proposals, not group consensus.
The distinction clarifies Beijing’s method. Katrin Kinzelbach found that China’s U.N. diplomacy contested the implications of human rights norms more often than their formal validity, especially monitoring and consequences for violations. Xinyuan Dai and Lucie Lu, analyzing more than 93,000 Universal Periodic Review recommendations, show that China increasingly champions economic and social rights, a preference shared by many Global South states. 
Rather than remove human rights, China seeks greater state authority to rank and interpret them and regulate the institutions through which they are invoked. Its people-centeredness is state-mediated and weighted toward performance rather than claims individuals can press against their government.
Which countries support China’s vision for global governance? The official counts require disaggregation. The Group of Friends began with 43 members in December 2025; by May, Wang said membership exceeded 60. The June white paper claimed nearly 160 countries and international organizations had welcomed or supported the GGI. These figures describe different degrees of association, not a verified bloc. Membership, attendance, support for reform, and endorsement of China’s full program are not interchangeable.
Even so, China’s argument is persuasive to many other governments because much of its diagnosis is accurate. Africa constitutes 28 percent of U.N. membership yet has no permanent Security Council seat. The IMF’s 16th quota review approved a 50 percent equiproportional increase while leaving relative shares unchanged. Developed countries first exceeded the annual $100 billion climate finance goal in 2022, two years late. OECD data put the 2024 total at $136.7 billion, but only about one-quarter supported adaptation and flows remained concentrated in middle-income countries.
The West’s selective legalism, expansive sanctions, uneven responses to war, and technology controls are experienced elsewhere as hierarchy in a new idiom. China makes strategic use of these fissures, but they would still exist without the propaganda. An argument can be opportunistic and still identify a real failure.
That is not to say that the developing world is in lock-step with China. The Global South is not a constituency awaiting a leader. Governments may welcome Chinese finance, demand Security Council reform, oppose unilateral coercion, resist Chinese maritime claims, and preserve strategic autonomy simultaneously. 
From Interpretation to Institutional Practice
The GGI matters because Beijing is building channels through which interpretation becomes practice. The United Nations supplies universal standing and authoritative vocabulary. The SCO, BRICS, the Group of 77 plus China, and the Group of Friends offer venues for coalition-building and agenda preparation. Sectoral bodies can translate principles into standards, training, finance, and bureaucratic presence.
Jack Taggart, Han Cheng, and Sebastian Haug described a comparable Global Development Initiative strategy as “institutional layering”: embedding new practices, principles, and alliances in established frameworks rather than immediately displacing them. WAICO offers an early illustration. Its influence remains untested, and one body does not constitute a parallel order. Yet it links U.N. legitimacy to a China-convened platform in an unsettled field, giving Beijing a durable address and agenda-setting capacity.
At WAICO’s launch, Xi pledged 5,000 AI training opportunities for developing countries, cooperation centers with regional organizations, and access for 30 countries to an AI-powered meteorological warning system. These are concrete deliverables, not the underwriting of an entire order. China may gain influence without assuming the full costs of leadership. The economic focus is also a vulnerability: a program promising “real results” will be judged by sustained delivery, not diplomatic uptake.
China’s proposal should be judged by the conduct its principles demand when compliance becomes costly.
Representation provides the first measure. Beijing is right to challenge Africa’s exclusion from permanent Security Council membership. Yet China holds a veto, and its public GGI documents do not specify how permanent membership should expand or how veto privilege might be constrained. Equality becomes persuasive when it addresses hierarchies from which its author benefits.

articles.title: India’s Communal Violence is Crossing into Nepal
articles.full_text:
With the RSS steadily building on Nepali soil, Hindu-Muslim tensions and violence are growing, especially in Nepal’s Tarai-Madhesh region bordering India
Screenshot of a video of a Vishwa Hindu Parishad meeting Dhangadi in Nepal on August 2, 2026, where activists shouted anti-Muslim slogans and called for the restoration of a Hindu state.
Nepal’s Tarai-Madhesh region abutting India appears increasingly prone to religious strife. With the sway of India’s Hindu nationalist groups like the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) steadily building on Nepali soil, the country is also witnessing more Hindu-Muslim tensions. While common in north India, such incidents had been rare in Nepal until recently.
Earlier this month, four Nepali youths were killed in clashes with police. The immediate cause of the incident was a Hindu procession passing through Dewanjung in Sunsari district, blasting loud music. The local Muslims protested. A clash ensued, police intervened and three youths were killed. (A fourth died in related protests in another district.) Local accounts suggest the Hindus in the area were already angry as the organizers of Muharram — a festival that marks the start of the Islamic calendar — had yet to remove some green pennants planted for the festival a month before.
According to one newspaper investigation, there were at least 17 such incidents of Hindu-Muslim tensions in the Tarai belt in the past eight years.
Earlier, Nepali Hindus seldom felt the need to publicly assert their religious identity. But as the Hindu forces in India started the rather brazen display of anti-Muslim activities starting in the early 1990s — most infamous of which was the 1992 demolition of the Babri Masjid in Ayodhya — the observation of Hindu festivals and rituals also began to change in Nepal.
By the time of the inauguration of the Ram Temple in India’s Ayodhya in January 2024, rooftop saffron flags had become a common sight in Hindu homes in the Tarai-Madhesh. As religious identities became more publicly politicized, saffron flags were increasingly answered by green pennants in Muslim households. Again emulating practices across the border, elaborate religious processions accompanied by loud music also became common among Nepali Hindus and Muslims alike.
The BJP’s rhetoric that all Muslims are basically anti-Hindu and must thus be resisted has also taken root thanks to the vocal advocacy of pro-Hindu, BJP-linked groups active in Nepal. They often cite reports of growing radicalization of madrassas in the region and entry of Rohingya refugees to justify their activism. The Indian security establishment under the BJP in particular has consistently pushed this line.
Nepal’s interim constitution promulgated in 2007 following the end of the Maoist insurgency had declared Nepal a secular state. Yet by 2015, the demand for a Hindu state had again started gaining traction. One reason for India’s imposition of a months-long blockade on Nepal at the time of the promulgation of the new constitution in 2015 was that the Nepali political class had ignored the BJP-led government’s wish that the new charter restore Nepal as a Hindu state.
Come 2026, the risk of the use of religion as a political tool is growing in Nepal. The country’s constitution bans the registration of political parties along religious lines. But if the polarization between Hindus on the one hand and Muslims (and even Christians) on the other keeps rising, major parties could face greater electoral pressure to more publicly embrace Hinduism: 81 percent of Nepalis are Hindu. There are already significant pro-Hindu state constituencies in all of Nepal’s major parties.
The 2015 constitution, while declaring that the country is a secular state, added the rider that secularism also means “protection of religion and culture handed down from time immemorial.” As the phrase is commonly understood to refer primarily to Hindu traditions, the provision gives the majority faith an implicit constitutional privilege.
This definition of secularism was a fudge to accommodate both pro-Hindu and secular constituencies. Yet such vagueness does not seem to be helping the cause of any community: A substantial share of Hindus want a de jure Hindu state; religious minorities, including Muslims who make up just over five percent of the population, feel more and more marginalized and want the Nepali state’s unconditional commitment to secularism.
The risk is that these sporadic clashes will become systemic and more difficult for Kathmandu to control. The Balendra Shah government’s handling of recent tensions left a lot to be desired. At the start, the incident in Sunsari was treated as a law and order problem and Nepal Police used disproportionate force to contain rioters—which paradoxically inflamed the whole region.
As communal tensions heightened across the Tarai-Madhesh belt, Prime Minister Shah refused to address the nation and appeal for calm. It was only when things threatened to spiral out of control that Shah finally addressed the country on the fifth day of the Sunsari police firing. Tensions began to die down the very next day.
But to maintain lasting religious harmony and preserve Nepal’s secular character, there must be broad political consensus in favor of separation of religion and politics. This can include an explicit commitment by political parties not to campaign on religious lines and greater representation of minorities in local administration and policing.
Unlike in India, Nepali political parties have a track record of setting aside their differences and uniting in the national interest during times of crisis. This time too all the major parties came together to appeal for communal harmony.
Yet when political competition becomes centered on faith, compromise becomes far harder. As India’s example suggests, parties can bargain over policies and power, but rarely over sacred identities.

articles.summary: With the RSS steadily building on Nepali soil, Hindu-Muslim tensions and violence are growing, especially in Nepal’s Tarai-Madhesh region bordering India

articles.title: From Jobs to Skills: Rethinking Vietnam’s FDI success
articles.full_text:
Despite its rapid industrialization, the country’s economy is not creating enough jobs that make productive use of advanced skills.
People riding motorbikes in Hanoi, Vietnam, Jan. 3, 2018.
Vietnam attracted $34.65 billion in registered foreign direct investment (FDI) in the first half of 2026, 61 percent more than the same period in 2025. At the same time, realized FDI reached $13.03 billion, its highest first-half level in five years. Observers including Harvard’s Growth Lab have also pointed to Vietnam’s increasingly diverse and sophisticated export base as a source of strong long-run growth prospects. By conventional measures, the country’s development model is working.
Despite this, another important labor-market signal has been moving in the opposite direction. Since the late 2000s, the wage premium earned by staying in school has been falling, with particularly marked falls for university graduates. This does not necessarily mean that education has become less valuable in itself. It may instead mean that the economy is not creating enough jobs that make productive use of advanced skills.
Whatever the reality, it has important implications for the Vietnamese government’s ambition of reaching high-income status by 2045. The gains from moving workers out of agriculture and into factories and services cannot continue indefinitely; future growth requires sustained productivity growth rather than labor reallocation alone. So far, Vietnam’s FDI model has succeeded on employment quantity but underperformed on occupational upgrading.
Drawing on 13 years of nationally representative Labor Force Survey data, a recent study that we conducted found that for every 100 jobs created in foreign-invested firms, an additional 100 jobs emerge in the same district – a local employment multiplier of roughly one to one. This is a large spillover, and a compelling reason why FDI has become such a central part of Vietnam’s growth story.
Foreign firms accounted for around one-tenth of total employment in 2023, up from almost nothing before 2000. Factory jobs raise household incomes and local spending, creating employment in other businesses.
The composition of these additional jobs, however, presents a more sobering picture. Of every 100 additional non-FDI jobs associated with foreign investment, roughly two-thirds are in services and only one-third in manufacturing. Most are generated by small, often informal household enterprises: i.e., the restaurants, repair shops, and retail stalls that spring up around industrial zones to serve factory workers.
Looking at the occupations themselves reveals the same pattern. For every 100 FDI jobs, only about 13 to 15 additional high-skilled cognitive jobs emerge, compared with 41 to 45 blue-collar production jobs and 27 to 31 clerical or service positions. The educational profile of jobs created elsewhere in the local economy largely mirrors Vietnam’s existing workforce, in which lower-secondary education predominates. Put simply, Vietnam’s FDI-led expansion has overwhelmingly been a jobs boom built on basic schooling rather than a skills boom. That helps explain why the country’s impressive educational progress has yet to translate into equally strong economic returns to education.
Vietnam has continued to invest in education. By 2023, workers with tertiary qualifications accounted for about 18 percent of total employment. Yet the economy has struggled to put those skills to productive use. Manufacturing employed 25.4 percent of the workforce but only 16.5 percent of tertiary-educated workers. Just 11.5 percent of manufacturing workers held a tertiary qualification, below the economy-wide average.
FDI-intensive provinces generally offer higher nominal wages. But the additional wage premium is not larger for better-educated workers. Moreover, part of the apparent wage advantage may simply compensate for higher housing and service costs in fast-growing industrial locations. FDI can therefore raise wages without necessarily strengthening the financial reward for remaining in education.
This changes the choices facing households. When a reasonably paid factory job is available after lower-secondary school, continuing in education becomes more costly, especially for poorer households that cannot easily forgo an immediate income. Unless the economy creates more jobs that reward advanced skills, Vietnam risks experiencing a growing graduate mismatch, in which educated workers are pushed into relatively low-productivity services, progression through upper-secondary education slows, and the country continues to lose talent abroad.
The policy question, therefore, is how to make capital, technology, and skills complementary. This is not an argument against foreign investment. FDI has been central to Vietnam’s structural transformation, export growth, and employment creation, and will continue to be so.
But it does suggest that Vietnam should broaden its definition of high-quality investment. Registered capital, exports, and headline job numbers should be assessed alongside occupational upgrading, wage progression, firm-based training, technical and managerial employment, engineering and research functions, and durable local-supplier development. Policymakers should distinguish a local spending multiplier from a productive capability spillover. A new restaurant or transport job is valuable, but it is not equivalent to a new engineering team, supplier certification, or transfer of production know-how.
Introducing local-content or skills quotas would be risky, and flexible investors may simply respond by locating elsewhere. More promising are incentive-compatible measures that lower the cost of undertaking sophisticated activities in Vietnam. These include reliable infrastructure, industry-linked training, applied research support, innovation services, and predictable regulation. Far from abandoning labor-intensive FDI, Vietnam’s objective should be to ensure that investment shifts towards more complex tasks and creates ladders within and beyond the factory.
Another part of the solution lies in Vietnam’s domestic economy. Resolution 68, issued by the Politburo of the Communist Party of Vietnam in May 2025, identifies the private sector as the most important driving force of future growth. That is a step in the right direction, but its success will be judged on whether a wide range of domestic firms can acquire technology, discover profitable niches, and scale up their operations.
Domestic firms are indispensable to Vietnam’s economic future because productive capabilities become embedded in an economy only when local businesses can learn from foreign investors, supply them, compete with them and develop innovations of their own. Better access to finance, easier formalization, and fairer competition would allow young and medium-sized firms to experiment, invest, and hire skilled workers. Export-promotion and network-building institutions can help them find buyers, enter global value chains, and learn from international partners.
Education policy must also connect more directly to labor demand. Public-private training partnerships, apprenticeships, and jointly designed curricula can improve matching, but they should be evaluated by whether graduates move into jobs that use and deepen their skills.
Place matters as well. Industrial and urban policy should combine reliable infrastructure with universities, vocational colleges, applied research centers, transport, housing, and public amenities. Such clusters could attract more sophisticated activities and the mobile skilled workers they require.
Vietnam does not need to choose between foreign investment and domestic enterprises. It needs domestic firms capable of learning from, supplying and eventually competing alongside foreign investors; and foreign investors whose success increasingly depends on Vietnamese skills and capabilities.

articles.title: Thailand Pledges to Work Towards Myanmar’s Full Reintegration With ASEAN
articles.full_text:
The pledge came as Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul hosted the country’s military-appointed president, Min Aung Hlaing, in Bangkok.
Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing walk past a guard of honor in Bangkok, Thailand, Aug. 6, 2026.
Thailand has affirmed its intention to bring Myanmar back into the ASEAN fold, following a meeting between Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and the country’s military-appointed president, Min Aung Hlaing, in Bangkok yesterday.
The summit was the highlight of the former general’s two-day visit to Thailand, his first official visit to the country since he led a military coup in 2021.
After arriving in Bangkok, Min Aung Hlaing was given a red-carpet welcome by Anutin, who then hosted him for talks at Government House in Bangkok. During the visit, Min Aung Hlaing also attended an official dinner, met the leaders of both houses of the Thai parliament, and spoke at a Thai-Myanmar business forum in the Thai capital, before departing today.
In a joint statement issued late yesterday, Thailand “reaffirmed its commitment to supporting and continuing to work closely with Myanmar for Myanmar’s full and equal participation in ASEAN mechanisms and processes.” Myanmar in turn “expressed its appreciation for Thailand’s constructive role in facilitating the normalization of its relations with ASEAN.”
In the statement, the two countries said they agreed to “further deepen dialogue at all levels,” in the areas of security, trade, and environmental protection. They also expressed their “joint commitment to achieve a peaceful and stable Thailand–Myanmar border.”
The visit saw the signing of three bilateral deals between the two nations. As per Nikkei Asia, these included an agreement on Burmese migrant labor in Thailand and another setting up a joint working group to address river pollution from rare-earth mining. The two leaders also reportedly discussed ways to boost cross-border trade, including the resumption of trade over the Second Friendship Bridge connecting the Thai town of Mae Sot with Myawaddy in eastern Myanmar.
Thailand’s invitation to Min Aung Hlaing reflects its determination to bring Myanmar back in from the cold, after five years in which the country has been barred from ASEAN’s summits. The reason for its exclusion is its refusal to implement the Five-Point Consensus, ASEAN’s plan for managing Myanmar’s ramifying conflicts. Agreed in April 2021, the Consensus called for an immediate cessation of violence, access to humanitarian aid, and political dialogue involving “all parties” to the country’s conflict.
For several years, Thailand has advocated engagement with the military junta in Naypyidaw, arguing that this is necessary to address issues like border security and transnational crime. This effort has redoubled since Min Aung Hlaing’s new “civilian” government took office in April. Since then, Bangkok has advocated a policy of “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar, and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow has also called for Myanmar to return to the “ASEAN family.”
During his meeting with Anutin, Min Aung Hlaing pressed the case for normalization, asserting that his government, which took office in April, was focused on ending the interlocking conflicts that have raged since the 2021 coup.
“Myanmar has now reestablished itself on the path to democracy and is moving toward a better future,” he said. “As the new government, we have now begun working on national stability, peace, and national reconciliation.” Speaking at the Thai-Myanmar business forum, he told attendees that they could “invest with confidence” in Myanmar’s energy, agriculture, manufacturing, and healthcare sectors.
Thailand’s invitation to Min Aung Hlaing has been roundly criticized by human rights advocates, who claim that it is undermining ASEAN’s efforts and helping the Myanmar military launder its international reputation. They have also pointed out that there has been no reduction in the frequency or severity of the military’s attacks on civilian populations since Min Aung Hlaing’s new government took office.
“Prime Minister Anutin should be ashamed to host Min Aung Hlaing, a murderous Myanmar military officer with the blood of countless Burmese on his hands,” Phil Robertson, the director of the rights group Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates, said in a statement. “When is Thailand going to wake up and realize that Min Aung Hlaing and his military compatriots are the core problem in Myanmar – and never will be part of the solution?” Aung Zaw, the editor of The Irrawaddy, wrote this week that Thailand “should not lend legitimacy to the thuggish regime in Naypyidaw.”
However, at a press conference yesterday after the summit between Anutin and Min Aung Hlaing, Sihasak rejected accusations that the kingdom is according legitimacy to Min Aung Hlaing.
“It’s not about legitimacy, it’s about reality,” he said, according to the Straits Times. “We have problems that we face along the border, and at the same time, we have to be proactive in terms of helping Myanmar on the path of peace, stability.” He added, “And the best way to achieve that is to have talks with those who are in the position of power.”
In any event, junta propaganda accounts on X gloated about the welcome accorded Min Aung Hlaing. “In accordance with international diplomatic customs, at the airport, there was a red carpet reception and a salute from the honor guard,” one account wrote. This, along with the official welcome ceremony outside Government House, “strongly reinforces legitimacy and paves a smooth path for bilateral cooperation,” it added.
How all this will play into ASEAN’s efforts to resolve Myanmar’s conflict remains unclear. The 11-nation bloc continues to demand action to implement the Five-Point Consensus (as does Thailand), and ASEAN’s special envoy for Myanmar, Philippine Foreign Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said last month that Myanmar’s full reintegration with ASEAN was still “far off.”
At the same time, Min Aung Hlaing’s government has moved from implicit to full-throated rejection of the Five-Point Consensus. In a speech on July 31 marking his administration’s 100th day in office, Min Aung Hlaing declared that the Consensus was “not the consensus of all ASEAN member states” and that it was merely an annex attached to a statement by ASEAN’s then-chair, Brunei. This came after the military-dominated Union Parliament passed a resolution rejecting the Five-Point Consensus as an unwarranted interference in Myanmar’s internal affairs, stating that it “does not align with the current political developments in Myanmar.”
The contending positions – ASEAN’s adherence to the Five-Point Consensus and Naypyidaw’s rejection of the same – would seem to be a recipe for deadlock. It remains to be seen whether Thailand’s policy of “calibrated engagement” will offer an incentive for Myanmar to begin even token implementation of the Five-Point Consensus, or merely provide the junta with a path back to regional respectability.

articles.title: How the World Learned to Live with the Exclusion of Afghan Women
articles.full_text:
The world has to do more than admire Afghan women’s resilience. It must stand with them by taking concrete actions.
Five years ago, when the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, the world watched in shock as images emerged of desperate Afghans trying to escape a country whose future had suddenly changed. For Afghan women and girls, however, the fall of Afghanistan was the beginning of a systematic effort to remove them from public life and rob an entire generation of their future.
Today, girls have been banned from secondary schools and universities; women have been pushed out of workplaces; and restrictions on movement, expression, and participation in society have expanded. Afghanistan remains the only country in the world where girls and women are prohibited from accessing secondary and higher education. More than 2 million adolescent girls have been denied their right to continue learning.
But five years later, the most troubling question is how the world learned to live with the Taliban’s policies toward women and girls.
Since August 2021, the language surrounding Afghanistan has changed. After the Taliban takeover, the world demanded the restoration of the rights of Afghan women and girls. Five years later, much of the conversation has shifted toward how to engage with the Taliban while raising concerns about women’s rights. The U.N. and other international community actors have adopted a policy of “principled engagement,” arguing that dialogue is needed to address Afghanistan’s humanitarian crisis while continuing to call for an end to restrictions on women and girls.
Engagement and diplomacy are complicated realities. Afghanistan is facing a humanitarian crisis, and millions of Afghans depend on international assistance. But there is a dangerous line between engaging with a country’s oppressive regime and allowing the systematic exclusion of half the population to become normalized. Consequently, the Taliban’s strategy has focused on waiting for global attention to its treatment of women to decline. Policies that once triggered international outrage have become just another item on the long list of Afghanistan’s unresolved crises.
The Taliban understood that controlling women’s lives requires controlling their visibility and silencing their voices. The restrictions began with education, but they expanded into broader efforts to remove women’s presence from public spaces, workplaces, media, and decision-making. According to the U.N., there have been more than 79 decrees and directives directly restricting the rights of Afghan women and girls since the Taliban takeover, while over 400 additional measures have indirectly affected nearly every aspect of their lives.
As a result, Afghan women’s voices have all but disappeared from public narratives. Afghanistan’s media landscape has faced enormous pressure since 2021. Female journalists have been pushed out, media organizations have operated under increasing restrictions, and public discussions about women’s rights have narrowed. UNESCO has noted that restrictions on women’s participation in media have tightened, including limitations preventing women from speaking on the radio.
This raises an uncomfortable question for Afghanistan’s media institutions: Are they documenting the reality Afghan women face, or are they, intentionally or not, contributing to its normalization?
Speaking at the Jaipur Literature Festival in London on June 6, Saad Mohseni, chairman and chief executive officer of MOBY Group, Afghanistan’s largest private media company, described conditions in Afghanistan as “normal,” stating that “women can walk around cities and drive without covering their faces.”
Yet while these remarks were being made in London, reports from Herat indicated that Taliban authorities were detaining dozens of women for allegedly violating the hijab rules – even though many were reportedly fully covered. The contrast between these accounts highlights the danger of describing life in Afghanistan as “normal” while women continue to face arbitrary enforcement of ever-changing restrictions.
Media organizations operate under extraordinary pressure in authoritarian environments, and survival often requires making difficult compromises. But journalism is about ensuring that the voices of those most affected are heard. When women disappear from newsrooms, interviews, and public conversations, their exclusion becomes easier to ignore – and easier to accept.
But the Taliban’s attempt to erase Afghan women has not succeeded completely.
Across Afghanistan, women and girls have created alternative pathways to learning. They study via online platforms, home-based classrooms, and private initiatives. Teachers who once worked in schools have become educators in hidden classrooms. Students who lost access to formal education have searched for new ways to continue learning. Thus, technology has become more than a tool for Afghan girls, it has become a form of resistance.
These efforts demonstrate the courage and determination of Afghan women and girls who refuse to give up on education. They have created lifelines for learning when formal pathways have been taken away. But no alternative program can replace a functioning education system. A girl should not have to find a hidden classroom, secure a device, or overcome extraordinary barriers just to access a basic human right. Access to education for all should be guaranteed.
The consequences of excluding women from education will affect Afghanistan for generations. UNICEF has warned that continued restrictions on girls’ education will have devastating consequences for Afghanistan’s economy, healthcare system, and future workforce.
The Taliban may believe that limiting women’s education protects their vision of society. In reality, it is weakening the country. When a girl is denied education, she loses the chance to build her future; her family loses the hope of a daughter who could become a teacher, doctor, or leader; and Afghanistan loses the talent and potential of an entire generation of women.
The Taliban closed school doors, but Afghan women have continued searching for ways to open them.
In the last five years, the world has repeatedly praised Afghan women for their resilience. They have been called brave, determined, and inspirational. But their resilience should not provide an excuse for allowing this injustice to continue. 
The world has a responsibility to take concrete actions: to keep alternative pathways to learning open while formal education remains restricted; to provide sustained support to Afghan-led education initiatives; to hold the Taliban accountable for violating the fundamental right to education; and to ensure that women’s rights remain central in diplomatic engagement and continue working toward the day when every Afghan girl can return to a safe and recognized education system.

articles.title: Where Is Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi?
articles.full_text:
Sean Turnell, an economist and former advisor to the ousted leader, returns to Beyond The Mekong to discuss recent events in Myanmar.
A stencil graffiti image of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi by an unknown artist in Bangkok, Thailand.
The military-backed government in Myanmar this week released four photos of the country’s jailed former leader Aung San Suu Kyi, who met with Arnaud de Baecque, the resident representative for the International Committee of the Red Cross in Myanmar, on August 3.
“This may be a first step, but it must not be the last,” her son, Kim Aris, said in a statement.
Sean Turnell, an Australian economist who worked with Suu Kyi and then shared a prison with her after the military coup in 2021, agrees, adding that “proof of life” is also required for some 20,000 people who are believed to be held as political prisoners inside Myanmar’s jails.
Turnell returned to Beyond the Mekong and spoke with The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt about the first confirmation of Suu Kyi’s existence in many years and the issues facing the opposition National Unity Government (NUG) and the various armed groups battling the military.
The NUG, its People’s Defense Force (PDF), and the country’s numerous ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) have faced a resurgent military this year and a counter-offensive aimed at retaking territory won by the rebels during 2023 and 2024.
Min Aung Hlaing, the coup leader and now military-backed civilian leader, has also gone on a diplomatic offensive in search of international legitimacy for his administration within ASEAN, which wants the junta to return to its Five-Point Consensus as a roadmap for peace.
Turnell, who spent 650 days behind bars prior to his release in November 2022, says the civil war, which has claimed some 100,000 lives, cannot be won by the military, as the NUG and EAOs continue to formulate a federal framework for a country mired by ethnic differences. But eventually, he says, peace will prevail.
